title: A wonderful phone especially for the new smart phone user!
text:
First of all let me qualify my five stars by saying this is my first smart phone so this review is not comparing the Motorola Bravo to another. I'm one of those people who said they never wanted a phone to be anything other than a phone. But I'll eat those words in this review and say that the Bravo is a great experience! People tell me it is a very clear phone to hear me talk which was an important factor for me. The on-line Consumer Cellular tutorials have been very beneficial to help me understand all that the Bravo will do. There is also an app on the phone called "help center" that lets you learn many things at your own pace.
The good things about the Bravo are many but I will try to mention a few that were such great things for me. Texting is much better on this phone and when you turn the phone sideways your big fingers can type much easier. The Motorola company has "MOTOBLUR" which combines emails and helps you in other ways that seem to make the Bravo the best choice for picking which cell phone to buy. I picked an android versus the iPhone and I am glad. The android market seems superior and works better with Microsoft based computers versus macs which are what I have at home and work. An example of "superior" is an app called "Call Control" that I have that goes through a list of marketing numbers and you can choose to have them go directly to voicemail at no cost so they don't call you. It's an interactive app where you can update marketing numbers so that others can block them too. I looked for this for my sister's iPhone and read it isn't available for those phones because Apple would not participate. The Bravo works on a 2.2 android system. I read a review that said a person will not know the difference when just starting with a smart phone and I agree. My phone is fast and efficient so I don't need to imagine how the 2.3 improves on perfection.
I also thought I would need to go with another company when I got a smart phone because of usage. I upgraded my texting amount and talk minutes to accommodate more than I need and the monthly cost is still only $41.00 which is less than one of the most popular unlimited carriers I looked into. Bottom line for people who haven't moved to a smart phone or for folks who are looking for a quality smart phone at a great price - the Motorola Bravo is a wonderful way to get started! I learn new things about the Bravo every day and expect I will enjoy it for years to come.

title: Started to worry after three days of usage
text:
UPDATE from April 17th, 2013:
For some reason, the camera has stopped saving images. It makes you think that the photo has been taken and saved, but then the file shows 0(zero) KB and no previews. Also, the original battery acted funky (showed a full charge but then discharged in 20 minutes) while an extra battery [[ASIN:B008H1IIPS SCUD®(code:1399, Hong Kong Stock) 1500mAh BF5X Li-ion Cell Phone Batteries for Motorola Defy ME525; ME525+; MB520; MB855 Photon 4G; MB525; ME863; XT320 Defy Mini; XT531; XT532; XT883 Milestone 3; Droid 3 XT860 XT862]] worked fine.

UPDATE from April 4th, 2013:
Now I can confidently downgrade it to 2 stars. The phone continues to be glitchy when it comes to voice calls. Motorola's support blames the network. This phone is OK for a teenager who sends 100 texts per day and makes only 1 call. If you need the phone for business or would like to avoid frustration because people do not hear you or you do not hear them from time to time, then look elsewhere. No wonder why after Google has recently purchased Motorola Mobile they laid off more than a thousand people and decided to close its Chinese division. I guess Google is hoping to replicate Apple's success by keeping the hardware and the software development in the same pair of hands. The head of their Android division was also moved elsewhere. Good steps that had to be done 3-4 years ago!

Anyway, due to all the glitches (despite factory reset efforts!) this phone should not be valued for more than seventy bucks.

UPDATE from March 25th, 2013:
I've purchased Blu Studio II 5.3 instead of Bravo. See my review here [[ASIN:B00B7NBOZE BLU Studio 5.3 II Unlocked Dual Sim Phone with Dual-Core 1GHz Processor, Android 4.1, 5.3-inch IPS Capacitive Touch, and 8MP Camera - U.S. Warranty (Black)]]

UPDATE from March 18th, 2013:
I am increasing my rating from 2 stars to 3.
The phone has not had its glitch with not sending voice (even with 5 bars and while sending messages) during last 10 days. Also, the problem with the Bluetooth pairing has finally been solved. Motorola Support was not able to help and neither Kia. The problem was with Android OS that was not showing Kia's request to get a permission to access the contacts list. The request was hid by Android in the notifications area.

UPDATE from March 8th, 2013:
I am lowering my rating from 5 stars to 2.
After three days of usage the phone stopped providing voice communication in both directions (incoming and outgoing calls). Motorola was always associated in my mind with strong signals and reliability (just recall those pagers that were dropped on the floor multiple times and continued working!). However, obviously Motorola has made a mistake of playing with Android rather than continuing with a proprietary OS. Android is a big disappointment.

After removing the batter the phone started to transfer voice again. But just think about it. If you have to remove the battery out of your car every day in order to drive to work, why would you buy such a car? Who cares about all the browsing functionality and apps if one cannot make a call? I've lowered the star rating to 2 because I think it is the most crucial feature in a phone. The phone that cannot make a call is not a phone anymore.

Speaking about apps, etc. It really makes me uncomfortable that just to start using the phone (or after the factory reset) one must create an account with MotoBlur. And in order to use the Android Market / Google Play one must have a gmail account. The car analogy can be applied here as well. We don't have to register anywhere in order to drive a car. Why, after spending a hundred dollars, I am obliged to register on multiple web-sites in order to just make a call? If manufacturers and Google think that they can impose anything on the end user, then I don't need a smartphone at all! I better stick with a simple/non-smart cell phone that I had purchased for twenty bucks several years ago. For thousands of years people have survived without cell phones and I should be able to survive too rather than jumping over the hoops after spending a lot of money on a gadget!

By the way, the quality of the photos taken by this phone is mediocre. It is not very noticeable while looking at the photos on the phone itself, but becomes obvious after they are transferred to a computer. They look slightly blurred (kind of like taken with a soft filter) and the colors are not saturated in red and yellow hues. Also, it does not take widescreen (16:9) photos or videos.

The vlingo (speech-to-text function for SMS/texting, etc.) was working well during first day, but then started to take longer time for "thinking" and now just quits and does not produce text results. I blame Android OS 2.2.1 rather than Motorola, but Motorola should make efforts to choose a better OS for its hardware.

I'll observe the performance of this phone for a few more days, but it appears to me that it is becoming a strong candidate for a return.

ORIGINAL post:
Ordered from Phone Etc vendor fulfilled by Amazon. The arrived phone was new in an AT&T branded box. A 2GB MicroSD card was already pre-installed inside the phone. The phone has arrived with Android OS 2.1 version, however, through MotoBlur it was updated the same day to 2.2.1 (took 15 minutes or so to download the update via Wi-Fi). Currently using with a T-mobile SIM card on a value plan without data. Test picture messages in T-mobile environment have been received and sent successfully.

The Android OS does not seem to be up to the hype. I had a PocketPC in 2001 and it seems that the Android OS has not made too much of a leap comparing to PocketPC. I expected more of a smooth usability experience that could be achieved during last 10 years (especially when Android is Linux based and not Windows based as PocketPC was).

A word of caution to those who are unexperienced with Android. Since Android is Google owned, Google is forcing you to create a gmail account (or provide info to connect to your corporate calendar) for such a simple feature as the Calendar. That is totally ridiculous! Although I am not doing anything illegal and don't need to worry about my calendar, it makes me uncomfortable that under the veil of convenience to the user Google (or any other mega-corporation) wants to own all of your information. Hence, I will try some offline (that don't sync with gmail) calendars that are out there and if none of them will be a good alternative this phone (only because of Android OS) will be going back to Amazon.

By the way, the reception seems to be good so far. Where a Nokia phone (3555b) would lose connection in our local Target, so far this one was showing 2-3 bard and maintaining its connection during a test call.

Will update this review after some more usage and after the search for an alternative calendar.

title: Decent smart phone
text:
This is my first smart phone. I've now had it for 6 months and I'm very satisfied. I bought it through Consumer Cellular, and their customer service was very helpful with setup. (I ran into a snag with initial setup because I live in an place with a very spotty wireless signal.)

I'm far from a techno wizard, but I was making calls, sending texts, and browsing the web right away. It took a couple of weeks of fairly intensive learning before I had everything set up the way I wanted it, but I'm now satisfied with battery life, freedom from intrusive notifications, etc. Consumer Cellular's instructional videos were very helpful for a novice user.

I did need to make a couple of calls to Consumer Cellular's support desk to get information on how to download a radio tuner that uses the FM antenna, but the app was free and it works well. A similar app is included if you have AT&T.

I'd never used a GPS and was amazed how much help it was on a trip to Philadelphia, a completely new city for me.

Occasionally I've had problems getting my Google calender to sync with the phone. Each time, I've fixed it by turning off the phone, and turning it back on in the presence of my computer.

The camera is better than on my previous phone, but not so good that it eliminates the need to own an actual camera. Outdoor pictures on sunny days appear washed out. I've been able to adjust them satisfactorily after uploading.

If the camera were just a little better, I'd give this phone 5 stars. Overall, it works as well for me as my sister's more expensive iPhone works for her.

title: Motorola Bravo - A Trusted Friend.
text:
I have lived with the Bravo for a bit over a year on Consumer Cellular. I take pretty good care of my gear, but this one has suffered a couple of hard floor drops, with no ill effect. It does everything I'd expect of an Android phone, including the easiest syncing I've done so far with the Google world.

My favorite thing about the Bravo, and most other Motorolas, is that it never forgot that it's a phone. In hand-held, Bluetooth and speaker modes, it is simple to use and delivers great fidelity. It is also great at grabbing weak signals. There are even tone controls for Voice Quality. You can adjust the phone sound to match your hearing and typical background. I've had smartphones that almost require you to use a Bluetooth earpiece, not this guy.

Also, as with other Motorolas, there is an available charging cradle with magnets that signal the phone that it's time to hold email alerts, etc. and make the screen look like a nice, digital nightstand clock. I'm a road warrior, and my standard call-home configuration is to use a Bluetooth headset with my phone charging in the cradle, aimed for best reception.

If you're looking for an Android to be your TV set, fireplace, or reader, Bravo probably isn't it, but if you want an indestructible phone with good battery life on Wi-Fi, once you set the controls, Bravo might be your trusted sidekick. When I wear this one out, I'll be looking for another.

title: I Hate This Phone with An Overwhelming Passion
text:
I hate this phone oh so very much. I bought the phone in April of 2011, and generally it worked ok from the start. The guy at the AT&T store did tell me that it was slower than the iPhone 3GS, but I figured it was just because he wanted to make the iPhone sale.

Boy was I wrong. Hmmm...where to begin. The majority of the time, the phone will just randomly drop a call, freeze during a call, and my absolute favorite, restart during a phone call. Replace phone call with a) Google Maps, b) gmail, c) Facebook app, or d) listening to voicemail and you have the bulk of my user experience right there. Also, while trying to send a text most of the time it just doesn't even work.

Very frequently it will attempt to load Google Maps, and then just stop. It will crash the app, then the phone, and the only way to get anything done is a force restart (as in, I pull off the back cover and pull out the battery). I have learned that the only way to use apps like Google Maps is to kill all tasks (the only reason why I keep Advanced Task Killer around) and then sit patiently for about 5 minutes while it all loads. WTF?

My absolute favorite is it's apparent lack of sequencing when it comes to apps. No, Motorola, I do not want to update every single app while I am watching Netflix, which then makes Netflix freeze, and you guessed it, I am forced to restart the phone.

I can not wait until I can get a new phone, and I will never choose another Motorola product.

title: My First Android
text:
I was influenced to go Android based on dodgy BB experience and very knowledgable friends sharing their experience. I have been very happy with the experience so far. May it live long! For this device specifically, I have been quite happy with the ease of use, nice build quality, solid feel, decent screen size and relatively good battery life. I also quite like the Motoblur interface, but not necessarily all of the AT&T preloaded apps which I can't use on my network.

That said, in the two weeks which I have been using the phone, I have had it lock up completely once. Also takes long to load contact list, which is a pain when in a hurry, or on the go. Screen sensitivity varies greatly, and not just the usual night vs. day variance I have found with most touchscreens, and have had the auto-rotation not work for a brief spell. Also have experienced some "ghost taps" on the virtual keyboard in very bright sunlight. All minor glitches which cleared up quickly enough, but I expected a bit more or less of it. I also would love the phone to have a cover on the mini-USB port to keep out the dust build up.

Overall a good phone, with great call quality and functionality.

title: Inexpensive good audio dated smart phone
text:

I've bought this phone to use on a pay-as-you-go calling plan with no data. I rely on mainly using Wi-Fi for data access while at home. The Wi-Fi reception on this phone is not that good. It only works well when you have good Wi-Fi signal strength. The problem with this phone is that it only has a 800 MHz single core processor and may take a little longer to load apps that happen to be heavy on resources. Occasionally, the phone may reboot unexpectedly when the app that you happen to be running crash.

Running most apps, the 1.5 amp hour battery generally lasts a couple of hours before you need to recharge. The nice feature of this phone is that it doesn't run hot when under continuous use.

The negative with this phone is that the transmit radiation level is almost at the legal limit. At the present time the firmware can be updated only to Google Android OS 2.2 and not to the latest one without rooting the device which will void the warranty for sure. The on board back facing non-flash 3 megapixel camera takes mediocre pictures and videos with audio. The color appeared to be a little washed out. I think the problem is just simply the low-quality small sensor and lens construction rather than the amount of megapixel on the sensor.

title: Good phone, not perfect, but worth it if you're new to smartphones.
text:
This is not my first smartphone, so I've seen how things can go well and not go well. This phone is amazing for social networking users, probably the best I've seen so far. The integration with Facebook, Twitter, and others is noteworthy and will serve you well. The only hitch comes in that it does import all your facebook and twitter contacts into the contact list. Which would be fine, except that not everyone lists their phone number on facebook (for obvious privacy reasons), so sometimes you have a contact list full of profiles with just email addresses. Something to watch for, but not gamebreaking.

It's highly customizable, courtesy of the Android 2.1 OS it runs out of the box, and as this is my first Android phone, I'm quite pleased with the OS-- I plan to stick with it for future phones. If you are an android power user (or at least enough of one that you care to root the device), be aware that rooting this thing is a chore, and there is no single easy tool to do it; you'll have to go command-line. Even then, the rooting did not work properly. AT&T also locked the Bravo from allowing sideloading, and even after I rooted the phone, it still did not let me install the Amazon App Store. Fortunately for those of us with this phone, Motorola was kind enough to put an app on the Android Market just for us Bravo users to allow sideloading (Search "Motorola Sideload Enabler" and find the one for Bravo).

I will warn you, also, that the thing comes with a goodly amount of AT&T Bloatware. For those of us who root our phones, it's no chore to remove, but I will advise those who do so to make sure your phone has the latest updates, because once you remove them, it becomes impossible to update.

However, overall, for the average user, this is an amazing phone that is reactive and integrated. I highly recommend the device for those new to smartphones, and give a good thumbs up for power users looking for a less-expensive android to tinker with.

text:
I purchased this phone from Amazon. It arrived promptly and exactly as described. The clarity of the color screen is unbelievable. Even in bright sunlight, you can easily see the screen details. The size is great - not too large, not too small.

The WiFi is a great little feature - especially for those without a data plan. I needed an unlocked phone that I can use when traveling between Canada and the USA and this fits the bill perfectly. I can pop in my SIM card for each country as needed which saves a great deal of money.

It comes with an micro sd card for extra storage. It senses when you put the phone in a pocket and locks the keyboard. It also senses night time and goes into a different mode to save the battery.

I purchased a Motorola phone as the last two Samsung models I had, stopped working, within months of each other. Time to try a different brand, in my opinion.

This phone has excellent video tutorials online at the Motorola Bravo site if you can't be bothered to read the instruction book (which I am guilty of).

The only con, in my opinion, is the short battery life with the GPS, WiFi, Blutooth, etc. all running. However, I am learning to disable some of the unnecessary features while out and about to conserve battery power.

title: If Only You Knew..........
text:
I have to chuckle when I read all the moaning about how outdated and pitiful phones like this are. If you want pitiful you should have seen my first radio; two transistors, AM only, thin metal and brittle plastic. Expensive 9 volt battery that barely lasted an hour, and yet it was
MAGIC compared to the tiny crystal radio I'd had for years before that.
Now days it isn't enough that smartphones improve every few months; where is the holographic above-screen mini-orgies? Better yet full size holo-decks controlled by super phone! Teleportation anyone?
It was years before the transistor found a use in AM radios and even more years before the first IC was born (with 2,300 transistors). Now the engineers are capable of putting more than 100,000,000 transistors on the head of a pin! What a time to be alive!
As for the Motorola Bravo; I say "bravo Motorola". I'd had a big expensive phone for more than a year and was ready to replace it with whatever comes next but it occurred to me that even the outdated Bravo would do everything I want done and it does. Made out of very durable materials it should last years and it only costs the equivalent of my truly pitiful two transistor radio back in 1960!
Update: I guess I'm not a "power user" and I definately don't want a huge screen phone that screams GEEK everytime I make a call on it, but I've yet to find this little phone lacking in any way. Even the 2.21 OS is entirely adequate. And one final item that may not even be available anymore--user replaceable battery. Now if ATT was equally pleasant to deal with!

title: If you need more battery life AND protection, this is the only game in town.
text:
I am a klutz. I drop my phone at least once a week. So I bought an Otterbox, which I used for 6 months. Loved it, but I could not use it with an extended battery. This became a problem, since by the mid-afternoon I was charging the phone from a power pack with the USB cord hanging out of the relatively fragile port. Then I saw the Trident Electra case with it's 3200 mAh battery. Hallelujah! Just as much damage control as the Otterbox with a big beefy battery.

But there were some caveats, for which I deducted two stars. First, the built-in screen protector has a problem - it adheres to the face of the phone after a few weeks of use, giving the appearance of water or oil between the two. Annoying, but not a deal breaker. Second, there is no belt holster clip, which Electra cases for other phones seem to have - a serious omission, and here's why. There's a silicon rubber "ring" that goes around the edge of the case to seal out dust and provide cushioning from impacts. It has flaps built into it to plug the earphone jack and the USB/HDMI jacks. If you attempt to slide the case into or out of an aftermarket holster or pocket and the USB/HDMI flap is not firmly in place, it can tear off, which is what happened to mine. Trident, unfortunately, does not offer replacement rings. You have to send the whole case back to them for a warranty replacement. But they did replace the whole case, no charge (other than shipping it back).

You can make your own belt clip. The holster I had was a standard ballistic nylon pocket with a top flap. I sprayed the fabric with some vinyl spray paint to stiffen it up and prevent fraying. Then I cut off the top flap and most of the front, leaving just a small pocket at the bottom. At the top of the holster I epoxied a couple of samarium cobalt magnets I pried out of an old pair of headphones, and I used some double-sided foam tape to attach a piece of steel plate to the back of Trident's case. This works quite well and the strong magnets hold the phone in place. Slide the phone up to easily remove it from the holster.

As I stated in the title, this is the only game in town if you want a bomb-proof case AND an extended battery for the Droid X/X2. Take some time to correct the major deficiency and the Electra will serve you well until your next phone upgrade.

ADDENDUM: Got my replacement case from Trident and you know what? It's not the same! Trident has addressed all the issues I had with my original case and then some. The new case consists of a silicon rubber body that surrounds your phone and the extended battery. Two plastic pieces clamp over this rubber surround. The entire unit feels really solid now. There's rubber at every place where you'd expect an impact to occur if dropped. The USB/hdmi port and headphone port now have thick rubber plugs that lock into place whether open or closed. They appear to be hinged for long life. The front panel buttons are absolutely a joy to use (although they still aren't translucent to allow the button lights to show through - no button flashing apps I guess). There's a fold-out kickstand on the back now for propping the phone up in either orientation (portrait or landscape), the screen protector no longer has the oily film look (at least so far), and THERE'S A HOLSTER CLIP NOW!. Bravo Trident! I now have no reservations with recommending the Electra case to anyone who needs long battery life AND protection from the rough and tumble real world. A well deserved FIVE STAR rating for this product and the company behind it.

title: Not a good phone.
text:
My review is kind of all over the place, but I'm sure you'll get it.......

I've had the phone for about 22 days now. The first thing Cricket told me was the phone should come with an SD Card, and mine did not. Without that SD Card, I was unable to do lots of things, like use the navigator, or download anymore apps, or take more than 15 pics and 3 videos. When I notified the seller, they were kind enough to send me an SD memory card at no charge. Once I received the SD card, I was able to download a few games, however, the phone kept saying error, force close or wait. So, I had to uninstall those apps, so no game playing for me. A friend of mine has this same phone, and the same thing happened with her phone. So, it's not just my phone, it's the brand itself. By the way, my friend got her phone for free with Cricket 3 years ago, and her phone did come with an SD memory card.

The other issue with this phone is the touchscreen is terrible on it. The top of the screen does not work, especially when the phone is turned 'landscape' style (side ways). Not one of the top or side buttons on the touchscreen works at all. I have to turn the screen 'portrait' style for it to possibly work. And this is when trying to text message or play a simple game that I had to uninstall because the touchscreen didn't work. Also, most of the time there is a delay when typing anything on the touchscreen. For example if you're typing a text message, and you touch the letter 'r', the 'r' shows up after about 5 seconds. It's quite annoying.

Another issue with the touchscreen, is when I'm in my 'apps' area, when I would touch slightly to select any app, it would not respond to that app, it would respond to a totally different app. When in my contacts area, anytime I select a contact, there is a picture of a phone and a picture of an envelope. Anytime I'd select the picture of an envelope to send a text message to that contact, it wouldn't select it, it would just dial the contact. There is another way to go about sending a text message, but the 'message' button does not work. This is obviously due to the fact, that the touchscreen is not good on it.

A few more things, last but not least, is when I finally received my SD card, I was able to send a video clip via email and text message. When that contact received that video, it was blurry and pix-elated. Another words, the phone video and pictures are terrible quality. The battery life on the phone is horrible. Apps on or off, services running or not, it doesn't matter, the battery life lasts less than half a day. The seller was kind enough to send me a new battery and charger, but it is still the same issue.

Don't waste your money on this phone. Now that I have to send it back, I have to pay for my own shipping and I have to wait to get credit to purchase a phone that works. By the way, my phone cost me way less than $70 with this seller, and now the seller raised the price to $72, what's the deal with that?

title: Love It
text:
I usually don't get along with headsets. The Jabra Supreme, though, suits me just fine. The voice quality is excellent. So far, no one I have called has noticed I was using a Bluletooth headset. The earpiece sounds great, too. It comes with two cushions; one projects slightly into the ear canal, the other rests against the opening of the ear canal. I prefer the one that just enters the ear canal because I think it helps direct the sound into my ear. Whatever cushion, though, the set produces good sound. No problems at all.

Fit: There is an adjustable plastic half-loop type thing that goes over the ear. I have never felt the Jabra was not securely attached to my head.

I also like the range. I tend to keep my phone on my person or close by. Even so, I have never walked beyond the device's range.

The controls, of course, are tiny. Nevertheless, I have no trouble using them as they are intuitively positioned and easy to press.

My only complaint is looks. The Jabra Supreme is one of the better looking headsets. It's not made to look like bling or jewerly or anything but what it is: an ear mounted commumication device.

title: Easy to use, good audio quality, no issues
text:
A couple of years ago, I purchased a well-rated Plantronics bluetooth headset. While it performed well, I was never able to get accustomed to the fact that it always felt like it was going to fall out of my ear (there was no clip to go around the ear), and I never was able to remember the steps necessary to turn it off, hang it up, etc. One blinking light can only do so much.

As a result, I rarely used it. That's a shame, as it wasn't cheap, and I'm sure that given enough patience, I'd probably get over the sensation that it was going to pop out of my ear and I'd finally remember how to operate it with confidence.

When this device became available, I thought I would give a bluetooth headset another try. I dislike holding a phone to my ear, and the fact that this model had an ear clip gave me confidence that it would work out. I didn't even realize the coolest feature until it arrived and I tried it out for the first time.

First off, the ear clip does what it's supposed to do. It keeps the headset in place and I never worry about dropping it. Audio quality is very good, and I've never received a complaint about my voice quality, and I've never had a problem hearing the person on the other end of the call. The flip-out microphone arm makes it very easy to turn on and off. A single large but unobtrusive (hidden in plain sight) button on the headset allows you to end a call without fumbling with the phone.

Now for the pleasant surprise and the coolest feature. Instead of a single blinking light that changes colors to indicate status, there is a voice that tells you through the headset what's going on. When it connects to the phone, it says "Connected" in a pleasant and clear voice. When the call ends, that voice confirms that fact for you.

Its ease of use and its performance earn the Jabra Supreme a rare 5-star review from me. It's not the most fashion-forward device, so you're not going to win any style points while wearing it. However, it does its job well, and it's easy to use while doing it, and those are the most important attributes in my book. This device is highly recommended!

title: Best of it's class
text:
Jabra has taken a different direction with the Jabra Supreme in that it doesn't utilize an in ear bud, but rather rests over your ear with a comfortable flexible ear hook. I know the Supreme has received some complaints about people saying it doesn't feel secure due to the ear hook being the only thing holding it in place, however if you replace the standard ear piece covering with the included alternative, you will have a much more secure fit. The alternative ear piece has two little prongs on it that DO go into the ear canal to help keep it in place. In my opinion, Jabra should have made this the standard version because without it, the Supreme does feel very unstable on my ear. That said, I'm ok with it not being a traditional in ear piece like so many other bluetooth headsets because over time those tend to really irritate my ears and I'm regularly pulling out the ear piece to rub my sore ear. Not fun. This new design is a very welcome change for me personally and I think it will be for many others as well. All these things considered, the Jabra Supreme is very very comfortable to wear and only weighs in at about 6oz. It might be slightly bigger than the standard, but I think for what you gain in call quality and noise reduction, the slightly larger design is well worth it.

The Jabra Supreme is also unique from most other bluetooth headsets thanks to its extended mic that folds back neatly for storage when not in use. Clearly the closer the mic is to your mouth, the better the other party will be able to hear you. This coupled with some really great noise reduction technology makes for excellent call quality, better than any other headset I've used for calls, bar none. When using the Supreme, people can't tell when I'm in the car or outside and that's really fantastic for me as I tend to make calls while I'm out walking my three dogs and wind can be a major annoyance with some lesser quality headsets. Not so anymore with the Supreme.

Sound quality is also excellent. You CAN use this for audio streaming, which isn't true with a lot of these single ear piece style bluetooth headsets. This is a nice addition for those times when I'm caught out without my Jabra Halo 2 and want to listen to some music while I'm working. It also looks more like I'm working and less like I'm listening to music than when I'm wearing a full headset, hehe! Nice bonus. It also has the dual pairing feature which basically means I can pair it to my iPad and my iPhone at the same time, and while I'm listening to music or watching a movie on my iPad and my iPhone rings, my music/video will pause and the call will transfer to the headset automatically. This is a common feature in bluetooth headsets these days but it's still very nice to have it as there are some bluetooth devices still floating around the market that can only be used with a single device unless you want to go through the hassle of pairing every time you want to use it with a new device.

The voice control is quite frankly the best I've seen in any bluetooth headset I've used in the past. You can control virtually any aspect of it's use with just your voice, even rejecting calls. It's quite nice to not have to fumble around with the buttons. Really the only buttons you'll ever have to push are the volume controls on the back of the unit. There is no power button because pulling out the mic turns it on and folding it back turns it off, much like the way the Jabra Halo turns on and off when you open and fold it.

Battery life is fair. I would expect it to be a little higher given it's size but it's fair enough. It will last for about 5 hours of talk time, which on some days really isn't enough for me but for the most part it is fine. It has a good long standby time however so if you use it infrequently, you can be sure it will keep its charge for at least a week with little use. Given it's design and superb call quality with excellent noise reduction, I can easily say it's the best single ear piece headset I've used and has become my favorite for making and taking calls. I still prefer my Jabra Halo 2 for entertainment purposes, but the Supreme more than fits the bill with it's extremely portable size and good battery life.

title: Buggy firmware installation reduces functionality.
text:
The basic design is a clever one -- pair this noise-reduction-savvy headset with a mobile phone app that allows more control over setting one's current sound/noise environment. Problem is, the headset, as shipped, doesn't have the proper firmware to function with the Jabra SUPREME mobile app. A series of instructions in the app tells you to go to the website, download new firmware to a PC, and install it to make the headset compatible with the app. Unfortunately, the firmware installation software is useless -- it repeatedly locked up my Win7 computer, and then I tried it on an older XP computer to see if that would work, and it actually crashed that computer. What are these folks thinking?

The app appears quite useful, though it doesn't always recognize that its own Jabra SUPREME headset is connected, and it's completely dysfunctional without the new firmware that can't be installed. The app allows 3 "coarse" adjustments to environments -- "Office," "Outside," and "Car," and there is a slider to allow the user to self-configure the noise-reduction to "Off, "Medium," and "High." Of course, all of these options are disabled because the app is incompatible with the outdated firmware. Quite a shame.

Even without the firmware upgrade and app integration, this is a solid unit. Sound quality and noise-reduction are good, but without the calibration options, it seems to opt for rather heavy-handed noise-reduction, and the result is a very thin, tinny, disembodied voice that just isn't up to par with the tech available here. Add that to the incredibly clunky ergonomics (the thing always feels as if it's falling off one's head), and it's uncomfortable with mediocre sound quality, though speech is very understandable with it.

Three stars because it just doesn't deliver what it advertises, and I'm honestly sick and tired of buggy firmware/software/etc. that hasn't been properly beta-tested. These companies need to get off of their collective behinds and make sure their hardware AND software works before foisting it onto an unsuspecting public at high cost. It's a shame because this could be a fantastic unit, and shame on them for ruining their own product.

Perhaps you'd think I should have filed a service ticket to get some help (and I may do that yet), but after receiving absolutely useless "tech support" before I filed my review of the vastly inferior [[ASIN:B005G2U80O Jabra EXTREME2 Bluetooth Headset - Retail Packaging - Black]], I didn't figure it was worth the effort and 2-5 day wait time before filing this review. If I learn anything new, I'll amend this review.

My suggestion -- if you don't wear glasses (and that's a big drawback on that unit), go with the [[ASIN:B004MCJBJI Jabra WAVE Bluetooth Headset- Black [Retail Packaging]] -- better sound quality (at least through my phone) at a significantly lower cost.

title: Didn't Feel Comfortable
text:
I have been using a Jabra Stone headset for my iPhone and have been reasonably pleased, but I wondered whether I would like a "higher end" headset better.

Much to my surprise, I liked the SUPREME much less than the Stone. It feels heavy and unnatural on my ear-- it didn't feel secure like the Stone and was constantly jiggling slightly as I moved my head. I was constantly annoyed by it and worried that it would fall off.

Sound quality, battery life, and features were all excellent, as you would expect in a unit of this price. I would certainly recommend someone actually try one on to experience how the headset feels on their ear before they consider purchasing it.

title: Fits the bill
text:
I've put this headset through a gamut of tests -- walking outside on a "calm" day to work, putting clothes away at home, and moving around in an office setting. In all instances, sound quality was clear -- even 20+ feet away from the phone (and through walls) and I never heard static. The other party never complained about not being able to hear me or even realizing I was on a headset. The ear hook is flexible and comfortable (for either ear) and the headset is darn easy to power on/off -- just open/close the boom microphone. I shook my head violently and the headset hardly budged. Judging by other reviewers, your mileage may vary on the last point -- but just realize you can bend the hook as much as you need to get it to fit your outer ear.

Most bluetooth headsets I've used have an earbud type mechanism to channel sound directly into your ear (which I prefer, especially in louder environments.) This unit does not, yet I had no trouble hearing my caller clearly in any of the above scenarios. Charging the headset is a breeze with the included micro-USB cable (and charger) -- and this is a very standard cable so you likely have one around at home already. Good move on Jabra's part -- you can use this with any standard USB charging accessory you likely already have (lighter, AC adapter, etc.)

A lovely lady speaks to you in your hear about your current call / pairing status -- a nice change to those used to memorizing "beep codes", though also a bit odd to hear a person telling you "call ended" all the time. The pairing with my iPhone 4 was a snap (this is rarely a problem with any bluetooth device these days.) Additionally, I was even able to stream music to it (mono, of course) and was impressed with the audio quality on something that's not even meant for music. The iPhone 4 also communicates directly with the headset you can see the battery life of the headset itself on your phone's screen -- I'm assuming this is some bluetooth standard, but I don't know its official name.

From the specs of the product, it should be possible to use the headset with multiple devices (read: another phone or computer) -- I haven't tried this feature as I have no need for it. It also apparently has some of it's own voice recognition features (beyond your phone itself), but always find these features downright time consuming to work right -- I can tap twice on my iPhone in half the time and generally get the same thing done. Even with a headset, I rarely am on the phone while driving so this is a non-issue for me.

For a high quality bluetooth headset, the price seems about right. Jabra seems to have nailed down the most requested features with an easy to use headset.

title: Convenient for the car
text:
I try not to talk on my cell phone when I'm in the car. If I get an important call, I tend to pull over. However, sometimes on long hauls I need to communicate, and for those I can't say enough nice things about the Jabra Supreme.

It's comfortable, connects easily (it even tells you how with voice) and has some decent noise cancelling when you use the Android app. Controls are simple and to the point. I have had mixed success with the voice commands, but they do work if you want to spend time learning them.

I especially like that there's no power switch. You flip it open to turn it on, and you flip it closed to turn it off. I can keep it in my car, and just flip it open and connect to my phone instantly when I need it.

All told, the Jabra Supreme is an exception choice for road warriors or casual communicators alike. Personally, I think a Bluetooth headset should be a mandatory purchase when you get a car, and you should have to prove you own one when you renew your license. Far too many idiots are on the road today with one hand on their cell phone and the other fussing with the car radio.

This is a simple, intelligent solution for those of you who insist on talking on your phone while driving. Isn't your life, and the lives of others, worth the price?

Update 4/2013: I just wanted to update and let people know that I am still using the Jabra Supreme, and it's still working wonderfully. I switched to a dumb-phone for a while, and the Jabra Supreme's voice functions actually work BETTER with it than they did with a couple of my Android phones! The Jabra Supreme still holds a long charge, still feels comfortable, and still makes it safer to drive and talk.

Update 6/2014: WAAAAHHHH! I lost my Supreme! I'm quite upset by this. If you get one, don't lose it... you'll feel sad about it for months.

title: One of the best BT Headset's I've used so far
text:
I don't use Bluetooth headsets as often as I would like. Mostly because I've never been able to find one that works well enough to use on a regular basis. I've been using Bluetooth headsets since they came out several years ago. But they're either uncomfortable, have poor audio quality, or just aren't reliable. At least until now... Apparently I've been waiting for something just like the Jabra SUPREME to come along.

My previous headset is the [[ASIN:B0009B0IX4 Plantronics Voyager 510 Bluetooth Headset [Retail Packaging]]] which I will be using for comparison. Because up until now this was the best thing I could find out there. The 510 works rather well, but suffered from intermittent connection issues and occasional poor signal quality. Otherwise it did work rather well; just not enough to really count on it 100% for an important call.

So on to the SUPREME headsets ergonomics. This is one area where I think they've nailed it. Unlike most headsets, this one sits comfortable on the ear with a soft plastic loop over the ear. There is a rubber cushion that rests against your ear as well. Most headsets are in-ear, which always get uncomfortable after extended use - at least for me. The boom mic is long enough to get it close enough to your mouth while not being too long. The boom mic also conveniently folds closed when not in use.

There are a few buttons on the device. The first of which is the big button on the side. This is what you'll use to answer/end calls. There is a small button on the boom itself to active voice commands and then some rather tiny Volume up/down buttons towards the back. Unfortunately these aren't the easiest to access on the go. But considering the limited space on such a small device, it's an acceptable trade off. The micro-USB port is also on the back, in-between Volume +/-. There is a rubber cover for the port, which will take some getting used to. At least while new, it's quite stiff and can be a pain to close. Hopefully this gets easier over time.

The headset features some nifty voice commands. You can use them to handle any basic commands such as pairing, making a phone call, or even checking battery status. Because of this, setup and pairing is about the easiest I've ever seen. The voice command also tells you who is calling via Caller ID, in case your phone doesn't already do this. I found this feature also simple and quite easy to use. I had no issues with it recognizing my voice and I can hear callers perfectly fine. This could be helped by the fact that it has active noise cancellation and noise blackout technology for the ear piece and mic. It is noticeable while in use and does seem to offer a slight improvement vs. a normal headset. People I've spoken with could still tell I was on a headset, but did say I was clear and easy to understand.

Another feature I use often is pairing with multiple devices. This allows me to pair with both my work and personal phone at the same time; which are both with me most of the time. One is a Samsung Galaxy S2 Epic 4G Touch (Sprint) and the other is an old Sanyo flip phone with AT&T. Both have no issues pairing or most importantly, re-connecting. If a call comes in, the headset connects right away without complaints. This is where you often run into issues with other devices. After your headset and/or phone are turned on/off, it's nice being able to pick up your headset and have it reliably reconnect to your device(s). For the past few weeks that I've been testing this device, it has done this flawlessly. This feature isn't exactly new as I used it with my old Voyager 510; but it is nice that it works now. :)

While these devices are small, they aren't exactly the most "pocket-friendly" things to carry around. Due to their odd shape, they usually get stuck or wont' fit comfortable in your pocket. Fortunately since there isn't an ear-piece protruding from the device and the boom mic folds closed, this is about as a travel ready as it gets. It's still somewhat bulky, but I've found it much easier to carry around. Once closed, the devices turn off. Open it, and the device powers on, ready to go.

Range is about what you'd expect for a Bluetooth device, up to around 30ft. After that you can expect loss in signal quality. As long as you stay within range, you shouldn't have any issues keeping a good signal. Despite having many other wireless devices around the house, I haven't run into any issues with interference or signal loss. Battery life has also been right about as advertised. About 6 hours talk time and 2 weeks stand-by. A full charge takes about 2 hours with a micro-USB cable connected to an AC outlet.

And now let's wrap this up with some Pro's and Con's!

Pros:
+ Very comfortable to use
+ Good ergonomics
+ Voice Commands
+ Reliable connectivity
+ Solid Signal/Voice Quality
+ Pairs 2 devices at once
+ Functional noise cancellation

Cons:
- Bit pricey at retail
- Smallish volume buttons
- Stiff USB cover

Overall I consider this Bluetooth headset highly recommended. While not the cheapest Bluetooth headset around, I think the features and quality make it justifiable. And considering you will likely find it cheaper on Amazon, it's a solid recommendation from me. It's something I have been and will continue to use on a regular basis.

title: An excellent modern Bluetooth Headset!
text:
I've tried a lot of Bluetooth earpieces over the years, with a lot of headsets ending up being clunky, uncomfortable and not very user friendly. So I was skeptical when I heard about the new Supreme from Jabra. I did my research and read all the reviews here on Amazon - not just on this particular model, but on about a dozen others too! I finally settled on the Supreme, and boy am I glad I did!

First of all, yes, this headset is noticeably larger than many other Bluetooth earpieces out there. Part of the reason is because this unit does NOT sit inside your ear, but rather outside the ear. This was a big plus for me, because I find earbud headphones and in-ear Bluetooth earpieces highly uncomfortable. I was worried that this earpiece wouldn't stay put on my ear, but the loop that wraps around the outer ear is surprisingly quick and easy to put on and it really stays put. Most importantly, I can confirm after wearing it for an hour in the car that it is adequately comfortable.

My favorite feature of this earpiece is how quickly it powers on and pairs with my iPhone 4. All you do to turn it on is open the boom. It powers up immediately, and within 2 seconds its connected. As a matter of fact, if my phone starts ringing, all I have to do is turn on the Jabra Supreme, hook it around my ear and it auto-answers! Very, very cool. It just works.

Accessing my iPhone's voice commands is easy too. Its as simple as pressing the large button on the face of the Supreme and saying "Phone Commands." It instantly activates the iPhone's Voice Control/Siri system and allows for hands-free dialing (among many other commands). No problems here. Again, it just works.

The volume buttons are really small and kind of hard to reach when the Supreme is on your head, but I'll tell you why that really doesn't matter. When paired with the iPhone, you can use the iPhone's physical volume buttons to change the volume on the Supreme. Not only that, but the iPhone also shows the Supreme's battery level at the top of the screen, next to the Phone battery level. I love this.

If I had to make a complaint about the Jabra Supreme, it would be that it doesn't come with a car charger. Not a huge deal though: you can always buy one from a 3rd party.

Audio quality is excellent too, by the way. I called several people and talked with them for several minutes before asking them how I sounded. Everyone thought I sounded perfectly fine. They never even knew I was on a Bluetooth headset.

Overall, I highly recommend the Jabra Supreme. Especially for folks that don't like in-ear headphones.

title: Works great on iPhone 4
text:
Update: Nov 2012
My Jabra Supreme had been working fine for 10 months, but lately it had developed issues that on only some calls that people heard choppy sound coming over from the Jabra when I speak. It seemed to occur at random calls. Turning on and off the Jabra to retry did not help. I contacted Jabra customer service. As soon as they got my purchase receipt, they sent a brand new replacement in a retail box via UPS under warranty. Great customer service. (By the way, Plantronics customer service is even better. They don't need a receipt. They just needed the barely visible code printed on the headset.

---

The Jabra Supreme works great with on my iPhone4. It is very easy to pair to iPhone4 and my other devices. The voice command is easy to use. All you need to remember is to press that voice prompt button on the bloom and say "What can I say" and the Jabra Supreme voice prompt will take you through the help section. The incoming and outgoing sound quality is loud and clear. I would recommend to anyone who is looking for a great quality headset.

Comparison to Platronics Voyager Pro Plus:
I purchased the Plantronics Voyager Pro Plus during a sales on Amazon last Dec. The Pro Plus has good sound clarity, but even at the highest volume, its sound level was too low. The ear plug never felt right no matter which size of the ear plug I tried. The Pro Plus also had a major problem with Bluebooth range - as several reviews on the Pro Plus had mentioned. If the phone is placed on the opposite side of the body, the Pro Plus loses connection. (And Pro Plus is a 3 year old technology vs the Supreme with its 2011 release.) I had sent it back to Amazon since it was just not usable in day to day situation.

The Jabra Supreme has none of these problems. The sound is very clear and loud (except when you are in a bar or in a room with many people talking - in which case I need to cover my other ear with my hand). The soft ear cup is comfortable (I use the one that protrudes into the ear canal) once you figure out how to put it on your ear with one hand. The voice clarity for both ways are almost excellent. I can hear clearly on conference with oversea calls (especially on those noisy phone connections from India :-)

Improvements needed:
- The voice command tab is almost flush with the bloom so it is a bit hard to locate when I am wearing the phone. A raised dot on the button, or a slightly taller button would work better in the next iteration of the Supreme.

- Unlike the Plantronics Voyager Pro Plus, the Jabra Supreme sound level is not entirely controllable or in sync with the iPhone 4 volume control. When the Supreme is first turned on, the sound level is in the middle range. Even when I turn the iPhone4 volume to the highest, the Supreme is still needs to be adjusted higher via the tiny volume button on the headset. To me, it is an annoyance not being able to synchronize the sound level between the phone and the Supreme as it becomes a 2 step process to adjust the volume - once on the phone, and another on the headset if one wants the highest volume. This is a nuisance when I am driving.

- Actual talk or listening time is not quite 5 hours as advertised. After 3 hours or so, the Supreme's voice command battery would announce 2 hours remaining, but it actually could go empty in in the next 30-60 minutes.

- Knocked one star off on the appearance of the Supreme. The Supreme voice clarity and ease of use are very functional, but the visual design is not that elegant compared to other Bluetooth products. I am a guy, so it doesn't matter to me that much. But I can image many users with discriminating tastes would be turned off by the odd industrial design.

But these minor design issues don't take away the good voice performance and Bluetooth sensitivity of the headset.

To keep it handy around me and not to lose it, I purchased a [[ASIN:B004BHX68Q CaseCrown Basic Neoprene Case (Black) to Protect Motorola H790 Bluetooth Headset]] on Amazon for slightly over $4. It comes with a belt loop and has a zipper (so you will be sure you won't accidentally open it as in some cases with Velcro strap type cover) . The pouch is the right size for me. My figures can fetch the Supreme with ease from the pouch. The main reason I bought the pouch is the belt loop. I can leave the pouch carrying the Supreme on my leather belt, so I always have the Supreme with me but not on my ear all day or worry about misplacing or crushing it when i sit.

I highly recommend the Jabra Supreme for those who need to do frequent conference calls with callers who have noisy phone connections oversea.

title: I prefer the Plantronics Voyager HD
text:
I have been a [[ASIN:B0027FFZEW Plantronics Voyager Pro]] user for a few years now, and in fact I own three of them (I spend a lot of time on the phone, so I like to keep many of them around so I can switch them when the battery runs out). I also gave two to my girlfriend, one to my brother and one to my best friend as gifts in the past. In my opinion, they are light, comfortable, reliable and they work *extremely* well.

Recently I acquired a [[ASIN:B005IMB5SG Plantronics Voyager PRO HD]] and that has features and sound quality that exceeds that of the original Voyager Pro. The Voyager Pro HD has become my primary headset.

I decided to try out the Jabra Supreme in direct comparison to the Voyager Pro HD (VPHD). I am very sorry to say that I'm not the least bit impressed with the Jabra Supreme. First of all, I found that the sound quality and volume level was lower than that of the VPHD. Second, I found the ergonomics of the unit to be inferior - while the VPHD is super-comfortable and effortless to wear as it rests balanced on your ear with it's integrated soft, rounded. rubberized form, I find this Jabra to be annoying as it hangs over my ear with only a thin, relatively hard hook which is sort of tacked on. The very unusual plastic ear cushion doesn't do much to isolate you from outside noise. Finally, the unit charges via a micro usb port which has a very annoyingly difficult-to-open cover (a cover which is rather pointless for a micro usb port in the first place). I just can't get excited about this unit - especially when I could be using my [[ASIN:B005IMB5SG Voyager Pro HD]] instead or even just one of my older [[ASIN:B0027FFZEW Voyager Pros.]] I just can't recommend this unit over either of them.

title: good, but not "supreme'
text:
I've had the Jabra Supreme for about a week (since seeing a blurb about it in the tech-toys segment of the biz section of the local rag). It's paired with my Motorola XT860. I'd rate the Supreme as "OK, but not 'supreme'".

I only ever used one Bluetooth headset, several years ago. That one, when it could stay connected to my earlier phone, sounded tinny, and was before the day of voice commands.
The Jabra Supreme connects flawlessly, but voices - both my outgoing and my callers' incoming - sound muffled and dead. Sound is understandable, but has a feel of being swathed in cotton wool. Most likely, I just need to experiment with the noise cancellation settings.

The Supreme is supremely comfortable. I can jog for miles with it, and forget that I have it on. On this point, I'm definitely at odds with at least one British reviewer. The foam pads are not the easiest thing to replace, but once you've persuaded them to grab, they stay. I have jug ears, and (apparently) an outer-ear-canal that spits out earbuds or doesn't like the feel of any that manage to lock in. The on-the-ear placement of the Jabra Supreme was just fine. It's light enough that it just nestled against the whorls, and laid the boom snugly alongside my cheek. In noisy environments, it seems to work well, though I've yet to try it while riding a bicycle (the wind noise...). Traffic noises were handled easily. Same for multiple fan noises in a server room.

Where I have a problem - and the other main reason that I bought the thing - is voice commands. It's been very hit-and-miss. I'd say I have a medium-timbre voice for a guy... I can't hit the base notes, but I ain't no soprano ... and I make every effort to enunciate clearly when talking to Miz Bluetooth, but I'm constantly asked to repeat commands. Or, she's mistaking me when I ask her to place an outgoing call - between "home" and "office" of all things. If I never again hear the phrase "please say again", it'll be much too soon. This morning, I had to say "Battery" four times, with increasing volume before she finally deigned to tell me how much charge remained.

Strangely, speaking more slowly and inserting a crisp pause between words is NOT helpful.

Often, I'll get as far as Miz Bluetooth (on the Supreme) querying the phone's contact list ... and the silence then stretches on... and on... and she ignores anything I say, so eventually I have to kill the (attempted) call and try again. It USUALLY works better if I just say the number. Trouble is that I don't have all my contacts' numbers memorized - that's what the phone contact list is for.

Strangely (yes I know I've already said that), when Miz Bluetooth is confirming who she thinks I've asked her to call, her own diction is loud and crystal clear.... until she gets to the actual name from my contact list, which comes out sounding like she's talking around a wool sock. This doesn't make sense, because it's her voice, not mine. All my contact stuff is text. None of the names were input by voice, so the phone is reading and she's passing on what it reads. The phone doesn't do this badly if I talk to it directly.

I have experimented with the angle of the boom mic, even switching ears, but while I effected a small improvement, I still find voice command recognition to be very spotty. The Jabra Supreme cost me around a hundred bucks, direct from Jabra's fulfillment center. (I'm Canadian, and our dollar is roughly par with the American one.)

It's good enough to keep using, but if I lose or break this one, I think I'll try Plantronics next time around. But that's because I don't mind paying extra for better quality. At the current price-point of 75-to-100 bucks, I'd recommend the Jabra Supreme.

PS: Why does every device I own seem to have a slightly different USB/charger connector? Ack!

title: Great performance
text:
I have not notice any less performance compared to original battery. I noticed thought my Samsung was dying quickly because of applications not really due to battery getting old.
I installed easy battery saver application which fixed the issue. It automatically turns the mobile and Wifi off when the phone on sleep and turns on when you turn on. It also allows periodic sync intervals so you still get your emails and calendar items but not be connected all the time so it saves a lot of juice. My battery improved by almost double.
Also try to recalibrate your phone's battery because that also improved my Samsung galaxy s2's battery life.
How to recalibrate : let your battery die completely. Restart and let is shutdown. Repeat until it does not restart anymore. Remove battery for 90 seconds. Them charge without starting the phone until it is fully charged without interruption. Them unplug and replug until it shows 100 percent and repeat until you truly see 100 percent. Then you are done.

The second thing that could happen (this is what happened to me) the phone will just stop charging. title: Counterfeit battery.  Donnot take a chance on these cheap batteries
text:
I bought two of these for my phone and my wife's phone. At first they were ok. But after a few months of use, the phones started acting up: becoming unstable, losing signal, charging problems, phone would shut off unexpectedly from 40% charge or less.

I finally saw another review of these batteries, and I was sorry that I didn't pay attention to the reviews when I bought the batteries . I finally put the original batteries back in the phones and the phones are behaving as expected--charging at a steady rate and discharging steadily.

I did weigh the batteries and the original weighs 40 grams. The fakes weigh 32 and 34 grams. I also peeled the foil off the pack and did not see the Near Field Communication (NFC) antenna coil anywhere.

The giveaway for these batteries was the swelling of the battery pack. I measured them and the swelling is about 30% in thickness.

I cannot express the frustration these two batteries have caused. I was charging the phone twice a day and still could not use it normally.

I just wish there would be a way to tell when a product is oem or a fake.

title: Quality not as good as original one that comes with phone
text: The one thing that sold me on the Galaxy phone was its great battery life. I could charge it once and use it for 3-4 days without even thinking about looking for a plug. Even with roaming wi-fi and travel, it was a real energy saving device. After more than a year of this comfort, the battery needed to be charged daily and I thought it was time to get a new one and use the old one as a backup. Amazon had a great deal with their price being only a fraction of what the others offered. I thought this was great because it was a green battery and affordable too. But the price is directly related to the charge level on the one I received. Its a battery and it works, but I needs to be charged almost daily. I am wondering if Amazon has some B-grade bulk deal on these batteries. Its okay and I use it alternatively with my old original battery and charge it up at the end of each day. But I am shopping around and talking to vendors to find out if there are different ratings and costs associated with batteries depending on their charge value. If I have to pay twice the price for a battery that lasts four times longer, the cost per charge value is actually less. It's too bad, because this is a terrific phone.Also, you have to be very, very careful to look for the 3-pin connector rather than the 4-pin connector which looks almost identical. This is why they show the picture of the battery in both the flat version and angled. I made that mistake seeing the other battery with 4-pins which fits the Samsung Infuse 4G. With an online purchase, it is extremely important to check the exact milliAmp hours (mAh) and the pin connector points on top. Amazon should identify how long between typical charges for their battery types. Again, I'd be happy to pay more for an extended battery life version as I travel for work and need this phone to make a living.

title: Good update to the iPhone 4
text:
I picked up a Verizon iPhone 4S on release day to replace my existing Verizon iPhone 4. It is an excellent, reliable device that excels in making phone calls, texting, emailing, and all the other stuff that one would expect from a smartphone. I have not had any of the battery life issues commonly reported on the web. I'm not sure if these issues are due to a bad batch of batteries or if it is a software glitch, but regardless of the cause, I have experienced no battery related problems at all.

The value of the iPhone 4S really depends on what type of phone it is replacing. For anyone with a 3GS or older or any other branded smartphone, this phone is an excellent choice. If you are in the same boat as me and already have an iPhone 4, the answer is not so clear. If I was limited to one new discounted phone every 2 years, then I would have stuck with my iPhone 4 and waited for next year's model. Fortunately, I have a family plan with multiple lines, all of which I pay for, so I am able to upgrade yearly without any pricing issues. I do not think the 4S is enough of an upgrade from the 4 to justify the upgrade if it means you will have to miss out on the iPhone 5 (or whatever it will be called) in 2012. Yes, the 4S is a little faster, Siri is pretty cool though not essential, and the camera is a tiny bit better, but other than that it's pretty much the same phone. I would wait for the iPhone 5.

Having said that, it is a great phone. The extra speed is noticeable. After owning the 4S for a month, I switched back to my iPhone 4 for a few days to see if I could notice any difference between the two phones, and the 4S is definitely faster. The camera is a bit better as far as getting less noise in lower light situations, but the 4 has an excellent camera too. I doubt switching from the 4 to the 4S is going to make a monumental difference in your pictures. If you really want better photos, save your cash and buy a book on art composition - improving your composition skills will make a much bigger impact on your photography than spending cash on a new camera.

If I could only pick one phone to have today, the iPhone 4S would be the one. But if you've got an iPhone 4, don't blow your 2 year upgrade on the 4S or you'll be kicking yourself when the iPhone 5 comes out in a year.

text:
Ordered the "new" product because the listing stated "Factory Unlocked by Apple, Never Opened." Inside of the non-factory shrink-wrap was masking tape on both ends. The original serial number sticker was covered over by a different serial number sticker for a similar product. Upon checking the warranty for the phone using the serial number, the Apple site said "We're sorry, but this is a serial number for a product that has been replaced. Please check your information and re-enter your serial number. If your information is correct, you may need to contact us." Since the serial number is correct, it's either a refurbished phone or a phone that has been used. There was no factory warranty as the listing stated.

Always check the warranty on the iPhones if you're buying a "factory unlocked" phone. There are a lot of people who will "unlock" an old phone and attempt to sell it as new. I did not open the package, but promptly contacted Amazon for a refund.

title: Best phone ever
text:
I was a bit skeptical. I'm on the tightest budget I've been on in my life and over the years thru tax times and gifts was able to save for a mac mini and an ipod touch 5, so to find an iphone of whatever generation that would work with what I already have is a boon to say the least and to have only paid $35 had me skeptical,as I said, but I have to say even as I've only had it for less than a week it's already the best mobile phone I ever had and right now the best overall purchase I've ever made.

Calls are clear. The screen is easy to navigate. Putting my face up to the phone doesn't disconnect calls like the last phone I had... Basics like that are key.

That said, it did come with what I would consider significant gouges on the screen... More than scratches... But with a tempered glass screen protector at 7 bucks, well worth the savings over new and the screen clarity is SO sharp that it's nearly unnoticable except when the screen is black.

The only other reason it lost a star is because I had to replace the recharging cord that came with it...also $7 on amazon... The one that came with it had a short and was temperamental about charging if it wasn't seated exactly right, but like I said, that was a cheap and easy fix too.

Based on reviews I was also a bit scared that I would have trouble getting it to accept my prepaid verizon plan as a replacement phone.

I made sure I went somewhere with wifi since I don't have internet and started the process. I freaked briefly when it kept taking me to a screen that told me to "connect to itunes", but I quickly realized there was a "back" button in the top left of that screen and pushing that got me to the right screen that walked me simply and easily through the process of changing devices.

Overall, I am VERY pleased with my purchase. Frankly, I'm glad just to be able to have a phone that works for my purposes.

It doesn't seem to have the ability to update ios past 7 but what's lost to that is mostly stuff I have no need for anyway.

title: Pros & Cons (with no cellphone contract)
text:
My wonderful 40-year-old son gave me his Galaxy Y GT-S5360 when he upgraded to a Galaxy S III 32GB.

As a retired software engineer I made it a hobby in my free time to snoop around. (I use it for emergency calls only, so I cannot comment on phone performance.)

Pros
I was pleased to learn it has both GPS and 'camcorder' video capabilities. I mostly use it at McDonalds and Starbucks to check email, play music, peruse Twitter and check the national USA news with a Wi-Fi connection.

Cons
• When using the Navigation app with the GPS it can take 5-10 minutes for it to find the address/location I've selected. Compared to my GARMIN nüvi 65LM GPS this one is quite primitive. But it does work.
• Small screen makes browsing the web almost a futile exercise. No wonder tablets are so popular.
• As others have noted, you cannot install very many apps before you've exceeded the internal memory capacity of less than 200MB. Very few apps allow you to move them to the micro SD card.
• This version of Android firmware will not work with Adobe Flash Player. So you cannot view many non-YouTube (non HTML5) videos on the Internet.
• Battery charge doesn't last very long and it tales over five hours to recharge.

Footnote:
In fairness to Samsung, even with its limitations, for the price ($90-$100) it is a satisfactory mobile phone.

title: Great phone, for the first 11 months. Then horrid.
text:
Edited:
I will leave the review as originally posted, but add this addendum. I do not recommend this phone at any price. It was a great phone for the first 9 months. Then it simply began falling apart. Tremendously unstable, and then at the 13 month mark it simply quit working. Just died.

The phone began having tremendous stability problems that were not resolved with a full wipe and restore towards the end of the warrant life. I had nothing but increasing frustration with the microphone on the phone. Callers reported huge issues hearing me. The smallest piece of dust and usual day to day dirt could clog the microphone making it unusable except in speakerphone mode. It froze up all the time during calls, answering calls.

Last week, it spontaneously rebooted and restarted into the recovery mode. The down volume key was apparently stuck, causing this. The phone could not be fixed. It simply quit working.

Avoid this phone at all costs.

Original review follows:
---

You cannot find a better phone for the money. Period. Add a good value on the Boost service and you'll never look back to whatever overpriced plan you came from. I don't know why most people never think of prepaid. I used to pay well north of $120/month back in the day for unlimited service. This phone is fantastic. It's thin, solidly built, very brisk to respond, and absolutely brimming with storage space.

-=Things I like=-
It's got a nice, bright 4.3" diagonal screen. The touch screen is both durable and sensitive. I've used it with rubber gloves on and never had it fail to pick up a touch.

It comes with a 1ghz processor which is more than adequate for anything I've run. Full screen Netflix, no problem. About 95% of the games in the Android Market, no problem.

The operating system isn't too cluttered with a bunch of bloatware. It ships with 2.3.5 of the Android OS. You get some, but not a lot. There's Documents to Go, something called MobileID, and that's pretty much it. That leaves a healthy 2.25+ gig available onboard for application storage. It also includes a 2gb micro SD card as well, but I have yet to put a single application on the card itself. I have about 150 apps installed and there's still 1.8 gig remaining internally.

Battery life is decent. No better or worse than any other Android phone. 10-12 hours of normal use for me -- email, bit of web, few calls, etc..

Price is quite good. I paid over $200 about a month ago and was happy for what I got then.

One Click Root available for the phone. I updated my phone to the latest firmware (B08) which you can do over the air on the phone for some stability improvements. Then I downloaded the one click root app and had root in about 5 minutes. Absolutely slick. It's amazing what you can do with the Android OS when you have root. Free WiFi tethering for instance. Undetectable tracking programs if you lose your phone. Ad-Block. Being able to delete the preinstalled bloatware. And that's just the start.

-=Things that are okay=-
The camera. It's pretty lackluster. They claim 5 MP. Yeah, it has 5 MP. But it's not a good quality 5MP. You get a grainy picture you can enlarge more at 5MP. Shutter time is pretty unimpressive too. It takes a few seconds after you hit the button to focus and capture. It has autofocus, so those barcode scanner apps WILL work on it. The AF is slow. The camera LED is absolutely AWFUL. It creates such a ghastly tint on pictures, it's not even worth using.

Very few aftermarket apps and accessories. I found an case that was okay. It's a rubber case to protect against short drops.

-=Things that are absolute fail=-
Ringer volume is far too quiet as a stock phone. Even turned up all the way, it's still VERY quiet compared to some phones. I found an equalizer program in the market and used that to boost the volume and also amplified my ring tones as well.

No OEM or aftermarket batteries. The way smartphones chew through batteries, it's only a matter of time until you kill the battery. What do you do then? I guess throw the phone away.

XT9 text input. It's junk. I hated it. Swype is 100 times better. XT9 looks cheap, feels cheap, doesn't work, and just generally is an awful implementation. I use a free trace type app from the Android market to replace the phone.

Dialer itself is very clunky and irritating to use. Again, found a third-party market app to replace the stock dialer.

MobileID -- Boost and Sprint tout this MobileID program on these phones. It's basically a skinning app. They have all of 4 to chose from and they're all horrid. All it does is install some crazy launcher, a bunch of apps you don't need, hideous ringtones, and then add some wallpaper you wish you never saw. After I rooted the phone, this was the first thing I deleted.

---

Despite the ho hum parts, it is a fantastic phone for the money. Good solid feel, reliable, and speedy with lots of storage to play with.
