title: I'm pretty disappointed, maybe moreso than I should be
text:
I'm pretty disappointed, maybe moreso than I should be, but my expectation with Anker is that they get this stuff right. If I'm being honest, I'd give this product 2.5 stars, but i decided to round down rather than up, which I guess is telling in its own right.

So I bought this to be my ultimate charger, since I have 3 USB-C devices and a bunch of random micro-usb devices. But the real trigger that caused me to purchase it was that I recently purchased an XPS 13(9360). Based on the reviews I read, it charges it and everyone is happy.

Well, I got mine in and was immediately disappointed. Yeah, it charges my laptop, but the laptop complains that it is a 30W charger, so it will charge slowly, even with one of Anker's nice USB-C to USB-C cabkes. That really sucks. And I was really surprised. I was greatly looking forward to putting the original, packed in charger in a box in a closet.

It turns out that Anker had an older revision of this device(with the same product number!) that did charge at higher than 30W, but had other problems that some experts discovered.

My loyalty to Anker is shot now, so hopefully I can find a company that makes a solid USB-C charger than can charge laptops and all other devices without causing damage.

title: Fantastic USB C PD charger
text:
I have only owned this charger for a week; however this is one amazing charger. This will rapidly charge my Pixel 2 XL using the USB C to C cable that came with my Pixel 2 XL (shows "charging rapidly" from lock screen). It also charges my Anker PowerCore Speed 20000 PD (this is the same power bank as the PowerCore 201000 Switch edition - https://www.amazon.com/Anker-PowerCore-20100-Nintendo-Switch/dp/B07FNV5TTT/ref=sr_1_8?ie=UTF8&qid=1549034483&sr=8-8&keywords=anker+nintendo+switch - just without the Switch logo on it) in the advertised amount of time - 4 hours - when using a USB C to C cable. I bought two of these Anker PD wall chargers on sale and have one mounted under my desk at work and keep the other one at home. A strip of double sided 3M mounting tape is included in the box so you can stick it wherever you want; this is nice since it is on the larger side, so you can easily mount it on the side of an end table to save space. I decided to go with velcro instead so I can move it around or take it with me if I want.

Pros:
- 30w PD from the USB C port (USB C to C cable needed) fast charges all my devices
- You can charge your Nintendo Switch in handheld mode from the USB C port with a C to C cable
- two cable ties included in box, nice for cable management and for keeping things neat when traveling with it
- 6 foot power cable allows you to mount or place the charger in a convenient location, and power cable doesn't block other outlets on your wall plate or power strip

I really wanted it so I could fast charge my Pixel 2 XL (mostly at work) and also my Nintendo Switch in handheld mode (when on the go/away from home and from the dock). The PD port is nice to have at home too since, even if you only have 20 minutes, you can fast charge while getting ready to go out and have sufficient charge to get you back home later. Like most new devices nowadays, my Pixel 2 XL will rapidly charge up to 80% battery in only 20 minutes. It'll especially come in handy when I have guests over since I live in an older apartment and finding enough outlets for everyone to charge their phones can be annoying. With this, I can plug it in somewhere close-by and everyone will be able to charge their phones at the same time. The specs state you can charge some laptops with it as well, up to 13" or so, via the USB C port. Make sure you double check what your laptop needs before trying it. If I still had my ASUS Chromebook, this thing would be able to charge it.

I can't really say anything negative about this product. It's a bit bulky to carry around but if you're like me, you probably have a large backpack, so this is a non issue. It's not marketed as a travel charger, but it's easy enough to take with you if you need to. For me, the 6ft cable to the hub makes it a great travel charger despite its bulkiness because I can plug in anywhere even if the wall outlet isn't in the most convenient location, and I charge all my devices with it. It's also the only charger I'll need to carry with me, so even though it's bigger, it sure beats having to carry around three or even four different chargers. And seriously, you can't go wrong with PD. Once you go USB C/PD there's no going back.

This charger is the same awesome quality I have come to expect from Anker. If you're in need of an all-in-one USB C PD and USB A multiport hub, this is the one to get.

title: Simply a great charger! (with one really tiny caveat)
text:
So, I got this product probably over a year ago now. It has been working flawlessly since I got it (it is the primary charger I use at my computer desk, to charge my tablet and many other things like flashlights and USB battery banks). Performance is as expected, the USB type C PD output indeed charges at up to 30W depending on what the device being charged supports. Because the USB PD standard supports many combinations of currents and voltages, the charger will default to a "safe and universal" 5 volt DC output, only changing to a higher voltage once a negotiation process has completed where both the charger and the device to be charged communicate what voltages and currents they support. This charger is capable of supporting most if not all of the USB PD voltages, and to minimize the effect of voltage drop over the charging cable (since all cables have some resistance), it will output the highest voltage that the device to be charged says it can support. This is a very safe process because it is done according to a well understood standard, and I have not had a single device become unable to be charged as a result of using this charger.
As for what I intended to use it for, I recently got a Samsung Galaxy Tab S7 (a rather expensive but highly capable Android tablet that can in some cases replace the need for a PC, similarly to how a Microsoft Surface can), and it supports USB C PD charging of up to 30W. When I am not using that tablet away from my computer desk, I leave it plugged into this charger 24/7, using an Anker 10 foot USB C to USB C charging cable (I went overkill on the cable, it supports USB C PD up to 100 watts, but hey at least I won't have to buy another cable until this one wears out).
Additionally, I use this charger to charge many other things using the additional USB type A charging ports, at the same time as the tablet is plugged in. Things I have charged with these ports are USB battery banks (I have 2 Anker battery banks, one "PowerCore+ 26800 PD model A1375", and one "PowerCore+ 20100 USB-C model A1371", both charging as expected), a Bluetooth wireless headset, several Streamlight flashlights, and even my Xbox One controller (that I use with my PC but can also sync with my tablet via Bluetooth if I want to play mobile games with a controller, something that actually works more often than you'd think).
Of course, this charger is NOT very compact, and really only makes sense either as something you mount somewhere near a desk semi-permanently using the included Velcro patch, or if you want a one-stop charging solution for pretty much whatever you can think of that needs USB power or charging. I have 2 older Anker chargers that have USB C outputs that do not support USB PD, and I use one of them when I go on vacation to keep my Nintendo Switch, the tablet I mentioned, the USB battery banks, the Xbox One controller, and the wireless headphones all fully charged. The advantage is that since my use case means I need a lot of USB charging cables all feeding power at the same time, it takes up less space than a bunch of "single or double output" mains-voltage chargers. The disadvantage is that if you only need one or two USB charging cables at a time, you would probably be better served by a different Anker product that would end up taking up less room than this charger (and it's power cord).

Now I mentioned in the title that there's a caveat, and that it's tiny.
It's tiny because it will only effect you if you have USB powered analog audio equipment.
The only thing that I have that is powered by USB that does NOT play nice with this charger is my USB powered audio mixer (a tiny little thing that supports just 2 3.5mm stereo audio sources being mixed into one 3.5mm stereo audio output, and capable of being powered by either USB or 2 AAA batteries, so maybe this is more the fault of the mixer's power input circuitry and not the charger, which is another reason why I think this is such a minor issue), and the effect of them not playing nice is not "total equipment failure" in any case. It's merely a small electrical interference issue.
When that audio mixer is powered by this charger, the mixer's audio output will have a very easily detectable "electronic sounding noise" or buzz on the output. It is not simple "white noise" or the characteristic 60hz "hum" of a ground loop, instead the sound is a very characteristic and "sharp" buzz (most certainly not a "pure tone" not even a square triangle or sawtooth wave adequately describes it).
No amount of ground loop isolators placed on both inputs and outputs of the audio mixer would eliminate the noise, and the noise remained when all I had connected to the audio mixer was a pair of analog headphones (in other words the mixer was driving the headphones directly, which it is rated to do, with no inputs connected, and the buzz remained). Switching to a different source of USB power did eliminate the buzz, thereby confirming that this charger was indeed the source of the noise.
However, since I had left the previous multi-port Anker charger (similar to this one, but not supporting USB PD) in place on my desk and plugged in to my surge protector, I merely connected just the audio mixer to that charger, and all was well.

Yes it's expensive, but it was worth the money, as USB PD chargers with higher power were both not needed and often don't have enough ports, and the minor issue I encountered is something I'm willing to forgive because well USB power supplies aren't really known for being "audio-grade power" in the first place.

I bought this so that my family could charge all of their devices at the same time. It serves that function well, although the Power IQ ports won't charge as fast as Quickcharge 2/3 ports. Overall that isn't an issue since more devices are switching over to USB-C and Power Delivery.

That's where the issue comes in. Although the USB-C port is listed at 30W and all the phones I've tested on it say "Fast Charging" when they're plugged in, it doesn't charge at the fastest speed.

Using a Note 9 and an S9+, I've tested this charger with several other chargers and cables. Unfortunately, the Anker USB-C port doesn't hold up as well, although it still charges faster than a non-QC/PD charger.

Samsung Quick Charger (comes with the phone): 2800mA via QC2
Crave 75W 4 Port desk charger (60W to the USB-C port): 2800mA via USB-C PD
Anker 5 Port Desktop Charger (30W to the USB-C Port): 2200mA via USB-C PD with off brand USB-C cable; 2000mA via USB-C PD with Anker Brand USB-C Cable.
Anker USB-C Power Strip (30W to the USB-C Port): 1800mA via USB-C PD with either cable

So I'm not sure what's going on here. It doesn't seem likely that I got 2 defective products from Anker as I've used a ton of their stuff and it's all been high quality. Other than that, if you need USB-PD, I might suggest looking at other chargers.

title: Just another great anker product. Even better for travel. First one I've ever had fail on me.
text:
I've had a couple Anker USB charging hubs and they've all been great. Of the 30-something Anker products I own from charging blocks, charging hubs, wall outlets, cables, usb hubs, and headphones they've all been pretty great. I'm not saying they're the best, but I've had no complaints. That being said, after a long time of heavy use, this has been my first anker product that failed. FWIW, anker helped me troubleshoot and replaced the product when it was confirmed. It was an easy process.

This has been mounted to my desk and charges ALL my devices. Tablets, mirrorless cameras, phones, headphones, mice, baby monitors, gopros, drones, battery banks, gimbals, speakers, etc. For the electronically uninitiated that have been complaining that the USB-C PD doesn't charge their laptop and all the people who've upvoted them, maybe do some research. The PD is capable of delivering a max of 30W (20V * 1.5A). There are very few laptops whose charging blocks are rated that low. What you'll end up with is a laptop that last slightly longer than if you were solely on the battery as you watch the battery percentage decrease. AND that's only if you're using a USB-C cable rated for 30W and potentially has the necessary chips.

I also use this when traveling to other countries. One of the big selling points to me was that it uses an external power cord. That means that I can buy a cord with the country's matching power plug and only carry that and never need those annoying travel converters.

Regarding the failure. The blue light would sometimes go off, but the unit would supply power but at a much lower amperage. Honestly not sure what the issue is as I really didn't wanna have to tear the PCB apart, run a trace, and test individual components. I've included pics of the inside if you're curious. Upon initial inspection, all I can say is there's no bulging capacitors. That's not to say that one might not be partially failing, but it's nice to know that it might not be that.

Looking forward to buying the updated slim 100W version soon!

title: The standard ports don’t charge very fast (UPDATED)
text:
I like this product for its multiple USB ports and the USB-C PD port. I got this mainly to charge my iPhone XS Max. When charging it using the Apple Lightning to USB-C cable, it is very fast. However, when charging my kids 2 Kindle Fire tablets, its is very slow on the standard USB ports. I have an older dual charger from Anker that is much faster. I expected at least the same amount of speed with the multiple ports. I probably wouldn’t have bought this charger had I known. I would have bought a single USB-C port charger instead because the other ports aren’t very helpful. Now I only use this to charge over night when there is a lot more time.
The packaging and the build were top notch tho.

UPDATE 4/29:
After my initial review Anker reached out to me. I tried their suggestion of charging only the tablet with another cable. My findings were that when having nothing other than the tablet charging, I was getting closer to what appeared to be 2.4 amps charging speeds via the USB-A ports. I am not sure if it was because I didn’t have anything plugged into the USB-C port during this trial or not. I was able to charge a dead Kindle Fire 7 Kids Edition from dead to 100% in just under 4 hours. I am increasing my review of this product to 4 Stars because it is better, but I think that if you max it out with 4-5 devices at one time, you won’t achieve max speeds on all ports. I would actually give a 4.5 but its not an option. This would also be my travel charger of choice because it will charge every device I’d pack on a trip (camera, phone, tablet, wife’s phone).
I would also like to give Anker service a 5.0 for their quick response to my review and a strong attempt to make things right. They offered to replace my original product or find me another product that may better meet my needs. There are very few companies willing to ensure customer satisfaction like this. I have bought a few other products by them, and they’ve always been great. This show of good faith will only encourage me and hopefully others to consider Anker products over others.

title: Great charger that can charge a MacBook as well
text:
I've been a long time user of Anker power products and when Anker finally released a new multi-port charger with increased USB-C power output, I knew I had to upgrade. I first started with a 6-port USB charger and upgraded to one of Anker’s first USB-C compatible chargers, but I was disappointed to learn that it didn’t charge a late 2015 MacBook. When Anker finally released a model that could charge my MacBook, I knew I had to upgrade. Please keep in mind that this charger is for charger only and does not function as a USB hub.

Pros:
- Anker’s design continues to improve with this model. My previous charger had a flat, brushed metal face where the ports were located. This looked very tacky and I was glad it was hidden inside my charging drawer. While the simple, black plastic exterior of this charger might seem bland, I personally like the design. The charger has curved edges which make it look more robust and sturdy.
- This charger’s USB-C port finally charges my MacBook. I can’t speak to newer MacBook Pros, but my late 2015 MacBook can be charged using this charger. My previous Anker charger did not output enough to charge my MacBook, so it limited the usefulness of the port.
- The USB-C port can also charge a Nintendo Switch just like the included charger does.
- It provide enough power to keep my Eufy Genie on. I was glad to not have to plug another power adapter into my already crowded surge protectors, plus, I am able to keep the Genie out of sight by leaving it in my charging drawer.
- The ports USB power anything you could hope for. In addition to power my Alexa device, I also use it to charge PS4 controllers, my Apple Watch and iPhone, a Nintendo 3DS, a Kindle, etc. It can detect what your device needs and will adjust the power output of each individual port to ensure your devices are charging properly.

Cons:
- The available 4 ports might seem like a lot, but I have all 4 ports being used up. I have my Eufy Genie plugged in in addition to an Apple Watch charger, another Lightning cable to charge my iPhone, and a USB Nintendo 3DS charger. Before, I had a micro USB cable for charging my Kindle or game controller, but with that being dedicated to my Genie, I had to unplug something if I need to charge a USB device. The is a minor inconvenience, but it is still annoying at times.
- This does not power the Switch when it is docked. If you wanted to use this to power the Nintendo Switch dock like I did, then you will have to reconsider. I was hoping to declutter my surge protectors, but the USB-C port doesn’t output enough to power the dock. While this is understandable, I consider this a negative.

TLDR:
This charger can charge anything you could ever want, including a late 2015 MacBook and a Nintendo Switch (in handheld or tabletop mode only). The increased output of the USB-C port makes this much more usable for me than Anker’s previous USB-C equipped charger.

title: Works well, but a step back in design from older units.
text:
This charger does provide 30W of power on the USB-C PD port, and regular USB charging on the other ports, so I can say with fairness that it does do what it says on the side of the box. However, the build quality on this new "Speed" generation of chargers seems to have decreased a fair amount compared to Anker's previous products.

The older versions I have of these multiport chargers used to be made of a nice "soft touch" type plastic that made the unit feel really high quality in your hand. This new generation is made of regular old run-of-the-mill matte plastic. I wouldn't say that it feels flimsy, but it doesn't seem nearly as well made as the previous generations.

Aesthetics aside, the real functional problem with this unit is that the chassis is no longer a flat sided rectangular cube like the other PowerPort models were. They've changed the shape of the case so that the smaller sides of the charger are now rounded off significantly more on the corners. Because of this, the unit is no longer stable when standing upright on a flat desk and is easy to tip over.

It sort of stays vertical on its own, but it really wants to lean one way or the other, or fall over completely onto its larger flat side. They do include a piece of adhesive tape to glue it in place, but all of the other Anker chargers that I own stay upright perfectly well without the tape, so I'm not really sure why they thought this change to the case was a good idea.

It’s a fine charger and does the job well, but it could stand to reuse a few design cues from its predecessors.

title: Damaged my MacBook
text:
I do not know if this is the Anker policy or just a single incident, but this is what happened to me. I bought this product and plugged my 2016 MacBook Pro into it. The next morning I checked it and noticed that it did not charge my notebook, so I took it to work and found that my Apple charger would not charge it. Tried it on another charger and it would not charge. So I took it to the genius bar at the Apple Store and after they opened it up and worked on it for about an hour they told me it appears that the power negotiation chip was fried.

I sent email to Anker and they told me “no problem” send us the adapter and once we verify our adapter was defective we will reimburse you for the cost to fix your MacBook. They even paid for shipping with a non-trackable shipment method. After a few weeks I sent them email and they said the adapter was lost and they would not pay for the damages since they were unable to validate it had a problem. I eventually got a “token” gift certificate to Amazon; no where close to the $503 repair cost.

So If you have an adapter that destroyed your MacBook, burnt down you house, electrocuted your child I would think twice before I sent it to them.

EDIT: After Anker read this they contacted me, confirmed that my adapter was lost. They then paid for the damage to my MacBook Pro. I don't think they were real happy with the way the original person "negotiated" with me. So; I am happy now and consider it resolved.

text:
I have three complaints about this charger. Maybe four. First, in an age where everything plugs in via USB, this charger takes a charger with a round connector that isn't interchangeable with anything I own. Pretty minor, but still kind of annoying.

Second, it's SLOW. Definitely not the rapid charge I was expecting. This was my experience with both the Samsung S21 and S21 Ultra, though results may vary with different phones.

Third, I originally put this charger on my desk next to my computer monitor. When I place my phone on the charger, my monitor flickers on and off and occasionally stays off. I'm guessing the charger emits some sort of EM interference that's not playing nice with my monitors. So when I'm at work, I have to charge my phone somewhere other than my desk or risk one or both of my monitors not working. Kind of a dealbreaker there.

Finally, the charger seems to interfere with my phone signal. I miss calls and receive the same texts 3-4 times, but only when my phone is on this charger. If I leave my phone in the exact same spot off the charger, it doesn't happen. Again, this was my experience with both the Samsung S21 and S21 Ultra, though results may vary with different phones.

In general, I like the idea of this charger and I like Anker as a brand. I have probably a dozen other products made by them that are generally top notch. There are just too many weird quirks with this charger and it's not particularly good at the one thing it's actually built for - charging.

title: Coil Whine - High Pitched Noise
text:
I've noticed that both this and another Anker wireless charger that I bought have coil whine. People sometimes say this happens when using cheap cables with the wireless chargers so I specifically bought wireless chargers from Anker that included their cables and yet I still hear the high pitched coil whine.

Its a really high pitched noise that the plug makes when its plugged in. From what I read, its from converting the high voltage from the house's power outlet into something the charger can use.

Typically only younger people can hear it. I'm in my early 30s and it drives me nuts. So if your hearing is very good, be aware that you may hear a really high pitched sound around this charging pad.

title: Nice charging stand
text:
I like wireless charging stands because I can have my phone in front of me at my desk and it's easier to see the screen to check notifications or do other interactions while it's charging than if it were laying flat. I own 2 other wireless charging stands and I would say this is the nicest of the 3.

The good:
- Seems to charge my phone (iPhone XS Max) faster than other wireless chargers that I've used
- Looks like nicer quality - doesn't have a finish that attracts fingerprints etc.
- The lip on the bottom of the charging stand doesn't stick out as much as other chargers -- what this means is that while it's on the stand, it's easier to swipe up from the bottom of the phone to unlock it. Minor thing, but it's a nice touch that I noticed.
- Phone seems to charge nicely in either portrait or landscape orientation.
- Works with phone case on

The bad:
- Maybe there's a good/valid reason for this, but it's not apparent to me... it uses a proprietary power adapter. Other wireless chargers I've used stick with something standard like micro USB. Not a huge deal but worth mentioning.
- I tried to place an airpods pro charging case on this stand and couldn't seem to find a sweet spot to get it to charge.

Overall it's a nice looking, nice quality wireless charging stand that seems to work better than others that I've tried. I recommend it.

title: A great desk side charging solution for your phone
text:
Anker's PowerWave II Stand measures 3.5 x 3.5 x 4.5 inches and weighs 6.1 ounces. The PowerWave II features 'smart Charging' which 'automatically switches between 5W, 7.5W, 10W, and 15W charging' when the device senses the maximum wireless charging capabilities of your device.

What I liked most about Anker's PowerWave II Charging Stand was:
- True fast charging. Many fast charging pads are using older 10W maximum charging speeds. Today's fastest standard is 15 watts and the PowerWave II has it.
- Upright positioning. I like being able to monitor my notifications at a glance. With flat charging pads, you have to either reposition yourself or pick up your phone to check notifications.
- It comes with its own power adapter. Many charging stands manufacturers leave buyers on their own when it comes to powering their wireless charging stands/pads/mats. Anker provides one in the box that ensures users can reach 15W Wireless Fast Charging for compatible devices.

What I liked least about Anker's PowerWave II Charging Stand was:
- Anker uses a proprietary barrel connector to power their Charging Stand. They could have easily make a USB-C port and included one of the many USB-A or USB-C charging bricks they already make within this package. Instead, Anker went out of their way to make this product unfriendly for travel as losing this cable effectively renders the stand useless.
- No fan. While this stand doesn't get hot while charging I like to leave my phone within the case while it wirelessly charges and my device does get warmer than I would like. A fan would have alleviated some of the heat.

Overall, this charging stand from Anker makes for a great companion for your desktop as it is capable of the fastest Qi wireless charging currently available and allows you to check notifications at a glance. While I really like the PowerWave II Charging Stand I deducted a full point from my overall review for Anker intentionally designing the device so it isn't travel-friendly. Anker also failed to include a cooling fan which would have helped dissipate some heat while phones charge. Those issues aside though this is a very nice offering from Anker that gives you the ability to wirelessly fast charge right out of the box thanks to the included power adapter.

title: Fast charges Pixel 4
text:
I've been waiting for Anker to release a wireless charger that could quick charge Google Pixel phones and this one is finally it, fast charges my Pixel 4XL at full speed.

For Pixel owners, unfortunately features such as Sunrise Alarm are still tied down to the Pixel Stand, but for charging this will do it at full speed.

If you've had any other Anker products you know what to expect for build quality:
-The stand is sturdy and has a nice matte black finish that doesn't show smudges.
-The base has a circular rubber foot to keep it from sliding when you place your phone.
-This stand includes a wall plug in that can detach from the base, it isn't permanently attached thankfully.
-I've not noticed any heat issues. My phone with a case on it and the stand itself haven't gotten overly warm from charging. I have confidence in Anker's wiring, but you've got their warranty in the event you get a lemon.
-The wall plug is a little on the large size, you may have trouble plugging this into an overly-cramped socket. The cable itself is quite slim though, I was able to route it through my desk easily.
-The small blue power light on the base only illuminates when the phone is actually charging, thankfully not on all the time. I do not use this on my nightstand, but you may want to point the light away from you if you're trying to sleep. I do not find it to be overly bright, but be aware in case you were going to use this on a nightstand.

Overall I am very satisfied, if this is anything like other items I've bought from Anker I expect it to last.

title: "Intelligent Power Allocation" is super frustrating
text:
*this IS mentioned in the product description, so I guess it's my fault for not taking it seriously, but the note that says "to activate 60W charging, make sure that no devices OR CABLES are connected to the other port" is to be taken VERY literally.

What this has is not "intelligent". It's just a hard-coded rule of "1 cable = 60W, 2 cables = 30W. No exceptions"

If there are 2 cables PLUGGED INTO IT AT ALL, but only 1 device attached to 1 cable, it will only charge at 30W. This means if you want to use it to charge multiple kinds of devices throughout the day, you basically have to constantly plug and unplug 1 cable to manually force it to charge the 1 attached device at 60W.

This is EXTREMELY inconvenient if you're trying to use the brick in an outlet in a hard-to-reach place. For instance, my old Anker power brick was plugged into an outlet behind the couch, with 2 cables connected to it at all times - 1 lightning cable, 1 usb-c cable. My partner and I both have laptops with USB-C charging, so I figured I'd upgrade to the 60W brick so we could charge our laptops too while the iphone charger wasn't in-use.

Nope. Gotta crawl behind the couch and completely unplug the lightning cable if you want it to charge the laptop AT ALL. Can't even SLOW CHARGE a laptop without the 2nd cable unplugged - both laptops just see 30W input and refuse to accept any power draw from it.

"Charge 2 macbooks simultaneously" might not be a lie since I assume Macbooks will accept the slow charge.. but no Windows-based laptop that I've connected to this will accept a charge without the 2nd cable unplugged. Extremely frustrating.

"Intelligent Power Allocation" should mean "oh well there's no device attached to this cable so I can fast charge the 1 attached device" or "oh well there's a laptop and a phone attached so I'll charge the laptop at 45W and the phone at 15." Not whatever this is.

title: Good Device - Test results below
text:
I have a Lenovo Corporate Issued Laptop that comes with a 65W USB-C charger. I've seen it actually consume 60W while charging. I wanted this device because it's smaller and has two ports but wondered if the step down in power would be sufficient.

Just the Lenovo plugged in (other USB-C slot empty), the Anker was providing 19.5V 2.31A = 45W. Not bad. It's a step down from 60W but more than enough to charge my laptop in a reasonable amount of time.

As soon as you plug a lightning cable into the second port (even if the device is not connected to the other end of the cable) I saw my laptop charge drop to 19.5V 1.41A = 27.5W

So Long story short, if I am charging my iPhone on one port, I can get the 15W charging and the other port can charge my laptop at 27W. I also tried a Aukey Battery bank and had it charging at 17W on the secondary port.

This is a good device. I wish it were available in black though.

text:
I wanted to charge a phone and my 36w surface at the same time. I was going to be happy with a 30/30 split but this charger will shutdown one port if more than 30 watts are asked for on that port during dual charging. My power-bank stays under this limit by itself but not the surface. Power-bank and phone, no problem. Surface and anything else, nope. This limits the chargers usefulness.

I wish the charger would act as a gate keeper and limit the draw to a bit slower 30w charging instead of turning off and resetting occasionally, effectively doing nothing on that half. It's a safe failure mode I'd imagine, but limiting.

It'd be a super great charger if they'd fix this.

*Update* Anker contacted me and offered a Atom III that they'd thought would fit my needs better. If the new charger can handle two devices at once at the specification it is rated for there will be a second update.

They sent the Atom III and it did the trick. One 45w USB C port and one USB A with quickcharge.

title: UPDATED: Disappointing limitation on multi-port charging
text:
UPDATE: Adding a star due to Anker's outstanding customer service following up on this. Anker reached out about my review below offering to send me a PowerPort Atom III (45W USB-C + 15W USB-A charger) as an alternative. I declined since that charger can't do 60W via its USB-C port or 30W + 30W charging, both of which are charging scenarios I will need. They replied offering to send a single port 60W USB-C charger instead, which I accepted. Anker's products practically always exceed my expectations, with this product being a rare exception, but they have always had fantastic customer service, whether they're responding to pre-sale technical inquiries, working with me to replace the one cable from them that I ever ended up having a problem with, or now trying to make things right in this situation. Well done Anker! Original review below.

I bought this because I liked the fact that it could provide up to 60W of power from either port and 60W total across both ports. Unfortunately, there's a limitation about total output across both ports that became clear when reading the output specs printed on the charger itself and which I confirmed by testing. If you have a device connected to each port, then the output on each port is limited to 30W, no matter what. So for example, even if Device #1 was only pulling 5W, you still only have 30W available for Device #2, not 55W available. The only way to get 60W total output across both ports is if both devices are drawing 30W.

I also discovered another problem, which admittedly isn't Anker's fault, but which makes this power output limitation even more of an inconvenience. I had planned to use this charger in my living room where I would always have a Lightning to USB-C cable and a regular USB-C cable plugged in, so that at any given time I could fast charge my iPhone and/or charge my laptop. It turns out that the Lightning to USB-C cable contains an active chip that causes it to be detected by USB-C power sources even when there's no device on the other end of the cable. As a result, by simply having that Lightning to USB-C cable plugged into this charger -- again, with no actual device plugged into the other end -- I only ever have 30W available on the USB-C cable to charge my laptop. That is FAR from an ideal solution, and since I keep the charger plugged into a surge protector on the floor with the cables held captive with a cable organizer on my end table, it's not convenient to disconnect the Lightning cable from the charger all the time, so this seriously impedes my planned use case.

I really wish this had been made more clear on the specs, or better yet that Anker had been able to provide 60W total output across both ports even in other combinations, such as 15W + 45W. I normally give Anker products five-star reviews because they consistently produce high-quality, well-designed products, but sadly this one is an aberration.

60W is plenty to charge phone, headphones, and tablet, but the Surface Book 2 has been the challenge since it is rated for 93W (with discreet GPU). The Surface Book 2 charges properly (consistently above 50W) as long as it is the only device plugged in, and it isn't under high load. Charging high power devices may require a quality cable, and I'm using the "Anker Powerline USB-C to USB-C 3.1 Gen 1 3ft cable", but I have also tested successfully with some Anker 6ft USB-C to USB-C cables.

If a second device is plugged in while charging the Surface Book 2, the power will split between the two, and the SB2 will stop charging. This is what I would expect to happen give the SB2's power requirements.

I'm very pleased with this purchase so far.

title: Does as advertised; wish power allocation was smarter
text:
Tl;DR: great charger with the usual high quality that I expect from Anker, would highly recommend. But be aware that it only seems to do 30 Watts max per port if two cables are connected even if one cable is just dangling out of the port with nothing attached.

I bought this device to switch to USB-C for travel. I use a MacBook 15 inch with USB-C and an iPhone with USB-C charging cable. This allows me to travel light with one charger for both. Honestly thrilled with it for the most part, and it does the trick with the flexibility of 2 USB-C ports (there aren't a ton of multi-port USB-C options on the market right now).

The only bummer is that the charging power allocation isn't that smart. It has 60W which (while less than the stock Apple charger for the 15 inch) is plenty to keep me charging under light workloads and recharge overnight.

But when I connect my iPhone charging cable, it reduces the power to my Macbook to 30 watts which means it stops charging or charges incredibly slowly. I can work around this by plugging the iPhone cable into the Macbook directly, which means I still get 60 watts from the charger and then 15 watts passes through to my phone. It works fine overnight, for example, when I just want both to be charged in time for the next morning. But I just wish there were a way to limit power to 60 watts across the board so that a fully charged iPhone plugged into the second port (or even an empty cable) didn't halve the available power to my Macbook (this may be an issue with the USB PD spec? but in theory they could do the "halving" after a device was actually charging or even build a 68W rated unit and not halve the power unless the iPhone was really sucking some current -- hint hint ;)

title: Fixed 30w + 30w split, even if your devices need 45w + 15w
text:
I have a Dell XPS-13 and an iPhone XS. The fastest the iPhone will charge is 18w, the XPS-13 requires 45w to charge at full speed. When two devices are plugged in, this charger ignores the information provided by the devices about what they need, and just splits it evenly 30w+30w between the two sockets.

If it were better designed, it would use the USB-C PD information it negotiates with the devices to allocate power in a more sensible way - in this case, 45w to the laptop and the remaining 15w to the iPhone. Hopefully version 2 will be a little more intelligent.

Updated June 18, 2019: Anker Customer Support reached out and offered to send me an Anker PowerPort Atom III (B07PWC32ZD) at no charge. This is the 'sister' product of this one, with a USB-C port and a USB-A port. This does split the power 45w to the USB-C and 15w to the USB-A when two devices are connected at the same time. As an extra bonus, the USB-A port is 'PIQ 2.0', i.e. supports Qualcomm Quick Charge too. This is a much better fit for my current needs.

Anker rocks - quality products and customer service that cares whether you are happy with them. I wish more companies aspired to this level of customer satisfaction.

title: Fried my MacBook Pro USB-C Port
text:

Went to use today with my 2016 15" MacBook Pro (only device plugged into the brick, using the original Apple USB-C power cable). System profiler indeed showed 60W coming in. The battery status showed charging and the brick got very hot, yet the battery percentage dropped rapidly as if the notebook was running only on battery power. Dropping from 100% to 10% in 2 hours, the brick clearly wasn't working, yet continued to get extremely hot.

Now, the USB-C port on my MacBook Pro that was being used is no longer working whatsoever (for power, data, or otherwise). Maybe I got a defective unit, but in any case, will now have to send my laptop back for repair...

UPDATE 5/25/19:
Got my laptop back from Apple today, issue confirmed. Required replacement of wiring for fried port and a new logic board.

title: One Charger to Rule Them All
text:
This is one of the first 2-port chargers made with Gallium Nitride (GAN), which is more compact than silicon. It charges all the devices in my backpack: I carry a 2016 Dell XPS 13, 10.5" iPad Pro, Sony WH1000XM3 headphones, an iPhone X, and a ZMI powerbank, all of which are served by this one charger. With its 60 watts of power, it charges my iPhone X to over 50% in 30 minutes and the iPad to 2/3 capacity in an hour. I found no compatibility issues with my laptop. However, if I charge 2 gadgets at once, each one only gets 30W. That is normal charging behavior and not a defect.

It does not come with any cables, so you will need to buy USB-C to ______ cables separately. Stay away from the cheap no-name ones, they are likely to be duds. There are smaller GAN chargers, but they either have one port or deliver <60 watts. Only get this if you need it to charge a laptop, otherwise you're better off with a 30 watt charger. Additionally, GAN confers little benefit over silicon if you're not going to carry the charger with you.

title: $750 mistake. Fried my Google Pixelbook motherboard.
text:
I bought this 45W charger because the Google OEM 45W charger that comes with the Google Pixelbook is a poorly designed beast where any slight tug on the USB-C cord unplugs the charger from the wall I also wanted smaller chargers to fit within the plug-in cavities of my side tables. So I bought 2 of these 45W Anker Powerport Atom III slim chargers.

But only 11 days after using them charger, my $750 26 month old Google Pixelbook motherboard flickered, froze, and died. It is now a brick, except the battery charging LED circuit still works. Reverting back to the OEM Google charger does not revive the Pixelbook. Google tech support troubleshooting has confirmed my Pixelbook is toast.

Looking closely, the Pixelbook charging LED blink sequence indicates that the Pixelbook isn't getting enough power from this 45W Anker Powerport Atom III charger, which is strange, because I also have the 30W Anker Powerport PD1, which DOES have enough power for the Pixelbook. So what gives? The problem is that unlike the original Pixelbook 45W charger which puts out 3A on 5V, the 45W Anker Powerport Atom III only puts out 2.4A on the 5V line, whereas the Pixelbook 30W charger DOES put out 3A on the 5V line. And there is no mention of a 12V output on either Anker 30W or 45W chargers.

CHARGER COMPARISON:
- Google Pixelbook OEM 45W Charger: 5/9/12/15V - 3A, 20V - 2.25A
- Anker 45W Powerport Atom III Charger: 5V - 2.25A, 9V/15V - 3A, 20V - 2.25A, 12V - 0A
- Anker 30W Powerport Atom PD-1: 5/9V - 3A, 15V- 2A, 20V - 1.5A, 12V - 0A

So apparently you can fry the motherboard of a Google Pixelbook using it with a poorly-named "45W" charger that actually provides less 5V power than a "30W" charger. This was an expensive lesson to learn!

Time for some industry standards. It is inexcusable for Anker and other 3rd party charger companies to put out aftermarket chargers that do not conform to the USB-C standard for power requirements.

title: Burst into flames.
text:
Initially, I liked this charger, so much so that I bought one for my wife to charge her iPad Air. It's really fast and did a great job charging my One+ Nord N10 5G.

Until it didn't.

The plug mechanism, which folds for convenience, started getting loose. It still worked, so I didn't think too much of it.

Then, just today, I plugged my phone in while doing some stuff in my shed, where I have a power strip. After a couple minutes, I heard a crackling sound from the charger, and smoke started pouring out of the charger itself. Then there was a POP! sound, and the charger starter spewing flames! I yanked it off the power strip by the cord, and it hit the wall of the shed, which caused the housing top to break off. Thankfully, I was there, otherwise the whole shed could have burnt down, and all the thousands of dollars in power tools it holds. I've let my wife know she needs to throw hers away. This is not only a manufacturing defect, but a dangerous one. I think I'll be taking my business elsewhere from now on.

title: Great for the Steam Deck!
text:
I already have several GaN USB-C chargers that are capable of 65+ Watts, but even though they are all quite small, none of them fit flush in the Steam Deck case power adapter slot due to being too wide. The charger that comes with the Deck is itself quite small, but with the same problem.
This charger has the same specification (45W at 15V 3A) as the OEM Deck charger, and is slim enough to fit in the included charger sleeve along with a 1 meter charging cable, and still fit flush with the outer shell. The charger sleeve itself is quite thick even with nothing in it, and if you replaced it with a microfiber cloth bag it would be even slimmer (Pictured in this post is the provided charger sleeve).
The charger is a bit expensive for only providing 45W, when you can get a 65W charger for about the same price from other brands. What you're getting for your money is the low profile footprint and the reliability that comes with a recognizable brand (+ Anker provides an 18 month warranty on this product at the time of my purchasing).
As a dedicated Steam Deck charger, and occasional phone/laptop charger, it gets my recommendation.

text:
Motorola appears to have stopped making the vastly superior H730 for some reason, and replaced it with this cheap crap that appears to have been designed by an idiot who was given the non-working shell of the old one and told "Just make something that works, you have a whole afternoon to do it."

The buttons work differently, for no apparent reason. You can't mute calls. You can't do last number redial. To bring up your voice assistant you have to press twice. The volume buttons are designed to switch to "music" mode if you press them for one second, which is also what you're likely to do if you're trying to increase or decrease the volume, so what the hell Motorola? Sure, some of the other missing features like the ability to support two devices were niche. But the thing doesn't even let you know audibly if you hang up a call. I don't know what to recommend in its place, but this should be at the bottom of your list.

title: Metro by t-mobile works great (down grade rating  to 1 was 5)
text:
Revised Review:
Unfortunately, I am downgrading the rating from a 5 to a 1. Phone was terrific until we installed the update. Keep in mind we bought 2 phones the update broke both. Then, we could no longer use the headset speaker (the one that applies to hearing the call privately phone to ear.) Only speaker, bluetooth, and wired ear buds would then work for calls. For us, this was a show-stopper! We consider phone call functionality a core phone function necessary for life and to conduct business etc. A company that sells a phone, that cannot meet it's core function should not even be in business. We tried to resolve with customer service/tech support. This was a waste of time. Google searching the 'headset' issue revealed that this is a known problem for many updates and they still cannot get it right. This is a backup phone at best. Lesson learned!
original review
We bought a pair of these phones and I was at first hesitant to purchase as the reviews were mixed on this phone working on BYOP on Metro. During the registration process the tech at the service counter of Metro told us that a warning came up on the screen vaguely states with no real reasons: This phone is not supported on the network, we decided to ignore the 'warning' and requested the tech finish the setup. I'm so happy we did...the phones registered just fine. All features function as advertised. Now we have upper middle class new phones with amazing features at a great price. I love the fact that the phones come with screen protector from the factory, and shipped with an attractive clear protective case. We had already switched to type-c fast charge cables with our old phones. We also purchased micro-sd 128g for added memory. Don't be alarmed that the phone comes with different charging adapters for International travel...you don't have to use these, but incase you do want or need to use them; they included a us adapter to the international adapter. We just use our regular type-c power adapters and cables and stored the international ones in the box for storage incase we eventually travel.

title: Mid-range features for a budget price.
text:
This is a really good phone for a budget price. A big battery, full HD screen, snappy processor, and decent cameras in a budget priced phone were all things that I was looking for. 12 hours of screen on time is pretty typical. I would suggest getting the larger memory version with more storage. It's not much more money and the convenience will pay off later. I have an SD card installed but I am only using it for a backup. The speaker sounds better than my previous phones. It even comes with a clear case and a factory applied screen cover. But the Gorilla Glass 5 on the front and back should prevent most if not all scratches. Fingerprint reader and face ID are both fast. The only drawback are the typical ads you get in Redmi devices but those can be disabled. Having an FM radio is nice when going to the drive-in movies. Some have complained about their screen but mine looks great. I have been surprised at how well the cameras adapt to the surroundings and the macro camera is really fun to play with.
Edit: I recently learned that this phone supports HDR10 which looks amazing on YouTube and Netflix. I also learned that it supports full manual in photo and video modes.

title: A flip phone on steroids!
text: Pricey little beast. If I ever lost it I'd contemplate spanking myself. LOVE THE SIZE! When my old smart phone (OSP) stopped recognizing SIM cards, I purchased an unlocked flip phone (for under $40) to make calls and receive texts. The WiFi and apps on my OSP still worked, so I was carrying around 2 devices for several months. I LOVED the convenient size of that cheap flip phone. Thought long and hard about dropping that much cash on a smart flip phone, but I figured I could always take out a 2nd mortgage. Enough sarcasm about the cost. The Z Flip is a very slick design and has what I value the most - a compact size! Read all the reviews and compared with Motorola's offering prior to purchase. Feel I made the right decision. Only 2 negatives: (1) could NOT get the data transfer function (phone-to-phone) to work either via WiFi or cable. Tried several times - no joy. Since the Z Flip does NOT have an SD Card slot, I ended up transferring my photos from my OSP to my computer, then from my computer to the Z Flip. I had data other than photos on my OSP and had to find creative work-arounds, including typing in OSP data using the Z Flip keyboard, to get everything  on the Z Flip. After 6 plus hours, I'm up and running. (2) Samsung tries to push a bunch of unwanted functionality on you (in the form of Apps or Plug-ins). Just say no to Bixby (Google that) and the other stuff.

The weight is not bad, actually about the weight of my compact Sony - guess it's all in the battery.

title: Versatile charger for multiple wireless devices
text:
Although this is an Apple-centric device with a dedicated place for charging an Apple Watch, the other two Qi charging areas will support other wireless charging devices besides Apple products.

BUILD QUALITY/DESIGN:
This product has a premium feel with matte rubber exterior that will keep your devices in place. It is heavy enough so that it won't slide around on your desk or table.

This charger comes with a proprietary power adapter, and although the cable is fairly long, some might find it too short. It was just long enough for me to put the charger on my desk, and run the cable down behind the desk, and plug it into a strip on the floor beneath the desk. Because a proprietary connection is used, there is no convenient way to extend the power cable if you need to.

There are no lights on this charger to show that it is operating. This is good news for those who want to use it in a dark bedroom -- but it's not quite as easy to tell when your devices are properly positioned on the pads.

The area for holding the Apple Watch is magnetic and will hold the watch in place without issue. However, if you were to dump the charger hard enough, your watch could potentially fall off. Although it is perfectly adequate, I wish the magnet were just a bit stronger.

FEATURES:
You can charge up to 3 devices at the same time. One Apple Watch product and two other devices. There is an angled area to hold your phone and a good viewing angle, and a flat area that, although designed for a smaller item such as a wireless earbud case, will also charge a phone. You can have two phones charging at once, and one will not take away power from the other. The charger has enough capacity to charge all 3 devices simultaneously without any slowdown. (Fastest charging speed is 10W, but you may get less depending upon your specific device)

There is no additional USB port for connecting a cable to charge a hardwired device. This might have been a nice feature, allowing you to charge wireless and wired devices with only one "plug in the wall".

VALUE:
This is a premium product with a good build quality and feel. However, you could accomplish the same task with 3 separate wireless chargers for less money. It is nice to have it all in one item on your desk, and having one charging area angled to allow you to keep an eye on your phone is nice.

PROS:
* Nice build quality / premium feel
* No lights, great for use in a dark bedroom
* Can charge 3 devices at once without issue
* One angled and one flat charging area, either or both can be used for a phone
* Flat area can be used for wireless ear buds

CONS:
* Power cord is proprietary and if you need it longer, you don't have an option to extend it
* Power "brick" is a bit large
* No lights to ensure the devices are positioned properly and charging
* Maybe not such a great value, but the devices is from a manufacturer with a good reputation

title: Great Construction, Good Quality Power Supply
text:
Over the last three years I've tried at least 10 different iPhone charging docks and this is easily the best. Full wireless charging at full power (thanks to a correctly-sized power supply). The dock is properly weighted and uses high quality friction pads that stop it from moving around on the table/desk top. It can easily charge three devices at once. The AirPods area can charge a second iPhone if you want.

The surface of the dock is coated in protective silicon which is pleasant to the touch and will not scratch your phone/watch.

Unlike most of the other docks I've used, this dock properly shuts off power transmission when the device is charged - I never wake up to a warm phone.

The only nit-picky problem I have with it is something that all docks seem to struggle with and that is charging the phone through a bulky case. The interesting thing is that this dock claims to charge through cases which are 2 mm or thinner, and for the most part it can. However on more than one occasion I've set my phone on it, verified that it appeared to be charging normally, fallen asleep then been awakened by a rapidly flashing light (which the dock does when there's some problem with charging). When this happens I've noted that it's only after having successfully charged my phone to between 70-80%, and if I remove and replace the phone most of the time it will finish without any trouble. It's my guess that even though it *looks* to me like I've got the phone aligned properly to the charging pad that it's off by a tiny amount and coupled with my bulky case the power protection circuitry is being finicky about it.

Even with my nit-pick this is still the best iPhone/Apple Watch charging dock I've ever used. If you don't use a bulky case, then don't even hesitate on this one. If you do, you may be perfectly fine or have the occasional issue. If you sleep with by your bedside, you might want to consider taping over the indicator light unless you want to be awakened to it flashing when there's a problem.

title: Poor quality control leads to multiple returns
text: We purchased two of these Logitech units to replace our venerable Belkin plug-in nightstand chargers for our iPhone 11's and Apple watches.  Of the first pair, one unit works flawlessly, charging both the phone and watch overnight.  The second unit failed to charge the watch, with the watch returning a "This device cannot be used to charge your Apple Watch" message every time. The unit charged the phone perfectly.  We experimented with moving the Logitech unit to a different location, making sure there was no foreign objects near the charger, etc., but to no avail.  We returned the unit for a replacement, which arrived quickly.  This unit DID charge the watch properly, but failed to charge the phone!  The phone would chime normally when placing on the upright pad, and begin charging, then after about 30 seconds, the unit's status light would start to blink, and the phone would stop charging.  We again tried moving the unit to different locations, but the same issue occurred every time.  Interestingly, the horizontal pad meant for Airpods, would charge the phone to 80% overnight. We returned this (second) unit for a refund.  With two out of three units that we received not functioning properly, we cannot recommend the purchase of the Logitech wireless 3-in-1 charger.  Over the years we have used many Logitech devices, and this is the first time any of their products have arrived non-functional.

title: Great for $100
text:
I got this phone to replace a ZTE Blade I got for a friend who is pushing 70. She has TMobile service, and was using the MetroPCS 1st or 2nd gen Blade with a 6" display, USB-C connector, fingerprint reader, and 4000mah battery. The subsidized cost of that phone was also about $100, four years ago. Recently my girlfriend switched to Visible (Verizon CDMA), and got a Blade A7. This is a fantastic phone, but at $79 the cost was only about half its actual market value. Full disclosure, I like ZTE, and have owned both their cheap and flagship phones.
I tested this phone using an AT&T SIM with no data, depending on WiFi, so please take that into account.

First let's take a look at what's good on this phone...

-Camera, tested against a Moto Razor 2020, and the images were about the same. Exceptional for the price.

-Speed, this is a no name 8 core chipset, but did very well. Better than MediTek, and competive with Qualcomm 500 series. The lack of RAM was almost always the bottleneck. Again, exceptional for the prce.

-Screen, while average for a $200 phone, and poor when compared to a flagship, the screen looked to be about 500nits, and is very good for streaming applications. Washed out for everyday apps.

-Good stock software, the applications, and widget options etc, were well thought out, and designed to appeal to an entry level user.

The Bad- and the first two are really bad...

- USB Micro, which should be illegal on anything with "2020" in the same. The charging, as a consequence, could not have been any slower, and harkens me back to the day when a frantic friend with a walwart was always looking for an outlet.

-Battery life- with the 8 core chipset, the 3250mah battery can last a full day on a full charge with moderate use, but the Micro USB charging aims to keep it from ever reaching full charge.

-No 5ghz WiFi, again, how is this even possible in something calling itself "2020"? While the 2.4ghz radio is good, it is really slow. I was only able to get about 15mbps download speed with a 1000mbps wifi connection. It took four hours to transfer about 5GB of data from my other phone.

- No fingerprint reader. That is why this has Android 9, because it needs the pattern unlock. Now to its credit, the face unlock feature woked very well.

- 2GB system RAM. The 32GB of storage is great at this pricepoint, and phones costing 50% more come with 2 or 3GB, I would've liked to have seen more.

Verdict- This is the iPhone 10R for the Android crowd. It really has eveything a person over 60 could want. That crowd cannot figure out fingerprint readers anyway.

The over 60 crowd cares about the camera, the software, and watching Netflix on their phone. That is who this phone is aimed at, and for that consumer, it is an excellent choice.

For the rest of us, we just need to belly up to the bar and pay $200 for something like a OnePlus Nord N100, or something like that. Other phones near this price point from Motorola try to do too much, and are a poor choice for an older consumer. Nokia has entered the market at the low end too, but both of those options start at $150.

The Blackview A60, which is one of the few phones on Amazon that can compete at this pricepoint, does not even run full Android. If you only have $100, this is a really great option.

I bought this phone for my son, it was going to be his first cell phone. I didn't want to spend a ton of money because, let's face it, a child is likely going to break their first phone. I'm an adult and I've broken plenty of phones. This LOOKED like a great deal and I was going to put it on ATT Prepaid. First, the phone itself is great. If you can get it to activate on a carrier, this is an amazing phone for the price. I have a Samsung S9+ and this thing rivaled my Samsung in size and capability.

US BUYERS BEWARE: I tried to activate this international version of the phone on both US Mobile Prepaid and ATT prepaid. Both carrier said nope..it won't work. It started working on ATT's GSM network for about 5 minutes until I tried sending a text message...then I got a message from ATT saying "we're sorry, this phone won't work on our network." Now it's basically a pretty, wifi only device. Thank God I can still return it for a refund. Even tho GSM phones are unlocked, many of these carriers have updated their services and for some reason many phones which were once GSM compatible are now NOT compatible. This phone fits that description. The advent of 5g has changed even 4g and 3g network compatibilities which I don't fully understand but just know this phone likely wont be able to be activated on any network in the U.S.

title: A Great Phone Case! Fits Perfectly!
text:
How can you go wrong with a phone case made by Samsung designed specifically for one of their own phones?!

I tried several different cases by other companies, but none of them fit just right. This case however is great! It fits the phone perfectly and there are no gaps around the edges. The phone sits very snug and it isn’t loose at all. The buttons work as expected without any issue. It feels quite nice and isn’t slippery at all, making it easy to hold.

Just be aware. Since it is leather, it is more susceptible to scuffs and markings. I happen to like how leather looks as it ages over time though.

**UPDATE**
It's been 10 months now since I purchased this case. For the most part it's still in as good of shape as when I purchased it. The only issue I've had is with the opening on the bottom of the case where the stylus is stored. Since the top portion is so thin it has unfortunately split. Other than that this is a great case that I would still recommend.

text:

Shockingly, this case made by the maker of the phone has a very poor fit. While the materials are nice and the leather is soft, the bottom corners of the phone pop out of the case several times a day during normal use.

I just don't get it! I've bought about 7 cases for this phone, and this one is by far the worst fit.

I certainly would not recommend this product to anyone. Why pay the premium price point, when a 12 dollar case gets the job done even better and you don't risk the phone slipping out? Then there goes your 1500 dollar phone tumbling to the floor because the case doesn't hold it properly.

Quite frankly its pretty rediculous to have a product made by samsung that doesn't even work properly. I expected more from the name attached, but I won't make the same mistake twice!

title: Not Too Thick Reasonable Protection Worthless Kickstand
text:
The case hits the mark in terms of the tradeoff between case thickness and protection factor. It is thick enough to offer reasonable protection for your shiny new $1000+ phone, but not so thick as to impede wireless charging or sag your pants.

That all said, the kickstands are an abysmal joke. If you try to use the phone propped on either kickstand, the act of setting the phone down in any manner other than extremely ginger, the kickstand will go winging off into the nether behind whatever platform you'd intended to set it on. After rummaging around on your knees to find it, reattaching it, and trying again only to have it go flying off a second time - you'll know that these kickstands are pathetic. The original Note Rugged cases (eg for note 8) had a *much* more complex and durable (and more "snappy") kickstand that, while still removable, never came off when you didn't want it to. These kickstands are pretty well a waste of space. This is probably bound for return.

title: The good... and the not so good
text:
On the good side, it seems to me that this case should take care of an N20U rather well. The ribbed rubber sides are nice and comfortable to hold, they are thick and high enough to protect the screen but they do not interfere with a screen protection film. The back is perfectly flat, it is raised enough to protect the camera unit and your phone will lay flat on its back.
On the not-so-good side, the 2 kickstand plastic legs feel flimsy and cheap, I'm not sure if they'll last long. Anyway, you can only put your phone in a horizontal position, it is impossible to make it stand vertically, which would be great to be able to make some video phone calls. The plastic back also feels cheap and outdated. Last but not least, for the price paid, you have so many more choices to consider that this option goes way down on the list.

title: Great Protection!
text:
This case comes in one piece and is easy to put on - and the best part is that it is friendly with most screen protectors already installed, meaning the sides of them (even the ones that attach along the curved edges of the screen) will be left unaffected.

It has a textured plastic matte back and gripped sides, and is bulky enough to make the back camera bump flush so the phone won't wobble on flat surfaces anymore... and yet it doesn't add a ton of weight overall.

The rim around the camera is elevated a bit so it will even protect the camera glass, and the case's top and bottom from lips are elevated ever-so-slightly as well to prevent the screen from a direct hard landing face first. And wireless charging still works with the case on.

The only drawback is the kickstands feel a bit flimsy, and I would not either one to prop the phone up for extended amounts of time.

But if you are looking for solid protection for your investiment, this case does the job and more.

The stand clip will pop right off if you try this, it also pops off easily if you apply even the slightest pressure in the wrong direction while it's opened. This doesn't break the case as it's very easy to pop the clip back on, but it can be quite irritating and just flat out flawed if you bought this case thinking you could use it in portrait stand mode.

I would have happily paid another $10 or $15 for more sturdy stand in the back that doesn't constantly pop off.... If you're buying this case because of the stand, you're going to be VERY DISAPPOINTED, Samsung dropped the ball on this!.... However, if you're buying this case because you want sturdy sleek looking rugged protection that also gives good wireless charging, and a stand is just a bonus feature that you don't really care about (this is me), then you'll be irritated by the stand that pops off, but still enjoy the case.

title: Case feels great in your hands, but would the phone survive a drop?
text:
Ok, so I was a little hesitant based on all the negative reviews. However, if you look thoroughly through the reviews, you will see that a very large percent gave negative reviews because of the kick-stand. So I went ahead and bought it as the kick-stand was not a deal breaker for me.

After putting the case on, the case feels great in your hands, I tried the kick-stand and both sizes do actually hold up the phone if you're in landscape view. If you want the the kick-stand to work for you in portrait mode, the phone is too heavy and pretty sure you'll snap the kickstand right off. Not a big deal to me because if it's in portrait mode, I don't mind holding the device.

I think this case would protect the phone from a drop if it at least fell on its side/top/bottom or on the backside of the phone. I am a little concerned if impact was made with the camera as the camera and the case are pretty even. They did not leave a whole lot of extra room for the case to take the impact and not the lens. Same thing with the front of the phone, it actually almost feels as if the glass on the front would make impact before the case took the damage, which if you have a really durable screen protector you might be OK. Sorry guys, I am not wealthy enough to complete such tests purposefully, in the event it all goes very wrong. Haha!

Another thing I noticed is that the case picks up hair & dust SUPER well. I noticed the debris getting stuck in the grooves on the back and I also noticed it start to accumulate on the sides on the front of the case. This might not be a big deal to you. It isn't a deal breaker for me and It doesn't seem very difficult to wipe the case down quick. it is just something I noticed and thought it would be good to mention.

Overall seems like a great case, it feels good in your hands, the fast wireless charging works without needing to remove the case, the kick-stand feature for landscape viewing seems to work well enough you'd be able to watch a movie or stream YouTube videos, the S-Pen and charging port are easily accessed, the buttons on the side for volume control & power are responsive to your touch.

The only reason I deducted 2 stars was because of the uncertainty of how well this case will protect the phone if a drop does occur. Hopefully if someone ends up dropping their phone they will update the reviews and let us know if it survived. :)

title: Cool case until the most recent Samsung update
text:
This is not a case that protects your phone from severe drops. It's very thin, but does cover the back and screen.

When I woke up this morning, this case worked completely fine. I was happy with it. As soon as I did the update, it immediately stopped. I reached out to Samsung for help and they referred me to a service center and asked if I had a warranty on the case. I bought the case through Samsung for $50 and it lasted a little over a month.

That being said, that's not why you buy this case. This case is for people who want to cover your phone, but have s view access while the case is closed. It's a cool concept and it's executed well. My issue is that this most recent Samsung update (9/24/20) has made the case useless. The phone no longer registers that the case is on it, the screen doesn't lock, the s view only displays the lit screen. The update killed this case for me.

Hopefully Samsung will send a patch to fix this.

*Edit:

I posted on a Samsung forum about my issue and received some feedback from other users. One of them had alsodone the update and was not experiencing the same issues. Two of them mentioned that dirt had gotten in-between the screen and the case and caused a series of scratches on the screen. Personally, this really worries me, probably more than my initial issue. Another Samsung user said that he started to experience the exact same issue that I did. He said that taking the phone out of the case and putting it back in would fix it, but it would always happen again. He ultimately got rid of the case.

That being said, I would definitely suggest looking elsewhere for a case.

title: A Heavy Hitter until 2022 at least.
text: 2 complaints: The display can have accidental side touches and depending on the case the phone can heat up a lot during intense gaming. Everything else about this phone is Golden. I use my phone as my main multimedia device, and this screen makes that much more enjoyable. Amazing colors, no camera splotch or bezels... Beautiful. The stereo speakers are very good and do beat small Bluetooth ones. The camera quality is good stand-alone and great with Gcam(sans root). No problems connecting with Att or Wi-Fi. The fingerprint reader improved after a week and is now very good. Battery life is important to me, so I'll give you some realistic times. Straight Pub G level gaming will eat your battery after 4 1/2 hours. YouTube can do 7 straight, perhaps a bit more. A normal day with light GPS, a bit of gaming and YouTube, a stroll through social media, etc. normally nets around 7 1/2 to 8 hours with a possibility for more. Stand-by is good enough for this to be a day and a half phone. Hold on to the original charger like it was a part of the phone. No letting anyone borrow it, and no forgetting it in a plug somewhere. Go back for it if you have to, it's that important. The phone charges fast (Hour and some change) with its original cable and square, but on generic chargers can take nearly two hours to charge. This phone is a great buy, and you have the bonus of knowing the front camera can't spy on you. Notice how the pop-up trend went away so quickly?

title: Galaxy A71 5G S-View Wallet Cover, Black; Searching for Quality
text:
Galaxy A71 5G S-View Wallet Cover, Black is listed by Samsung as compatible with Galaxy A71 5G (US Cellular) and GalaxyA71 5G UW (Verizon).

While it is very easy to insert the Galaxy A71 5G UW SM-A716V(Verizon) into the S-View wallet cover, it requires a lot of manual dexterity to remove the cellphone from this case. Wear and tear is rapid. In less than two weeks, stress fractures appeared at the bottom reliable, rounded, side protection of the wallet cover. The best feature of the S-View wallet cover is the side cut-out that allows easy access to the Galaxy cellphone side buttons. There is no interference because of the side button variations associated with the Verizon branded Galaxy A71 5G UW (SM-A716V).

There are no instructions on how to implement the S-View feature of the wallet cover. If you reboot the phone in the wallet cover, the S-View feature is activated. However, opening the cover does not let you access the phone. This means, removal of the phone from the case and doing a hard reboot. In Settings/Accessibility, there is no listing for the S-View wallet cover. Therefore, you can neither configure nor access the S-View feature.

The problem with the implementation of the S-View feature is apparently unique to the Verizon branded Galaxy A71 5G UW (SM-A716V). Oh Verizon, how could you be so mean and why would you suppress a charming S-view wallet cover feature?.

Given the cost of this case and the name brand manufacturer, a basic quality expectation is that this product works flawlessly out of the box and has basic instructions for use. Yet, in spite of its warts and annoyances this S-View wallet cover, it is one of the few available cases that fit the Verizon branded Galaxy A71 5G UW (SM-A716V).Galaxy A71 5G S-View Wallet Cover, Black is a useful case which is the best of the barely existent.

title: Why?  Just why do they have such bad default settings.
text:
Samsung, please take note. Yes this phone is actually okay. My review and rating is based on the default settings. Why would anyone setup a phone as bad as this? To put it mildly the default settings are so bad you will end up on the phone with support for hours. That is not a joke at all. I spent hours upon hours removing, and setting up this phone so I could even stand it. By default the phone using something called Bixby and that's not a joke. Samsung in all their intelligence thought they could out do google and android. So the default settings are all Bixby and they even thought why would you want a power button? The default setting for power is to call up Bixby (not even joking)? So if you are an older generation you are on call to figure out how to even shut the stupid phone off.

It's at this point that I realize maybe I am older, maybe I just don't get the next generation. Why would the default settings be so bad, but it gets so much worse. You can't even turn Bixby off, or really remove it ever from the phone. Samsung why is this the default, I just wanted a new phone? Yes I get that new generation understand a million settings to get something right. Why would I have to spent so many hours / days just trying to get this to work I mean really? I am so frustrated, lost, confused, why wouldn't something just work like an android phone? This is my actual thought process, yes I am older.... I realize that now. This phone has made me realize I'm a programmer that has aged and I am questioning my own existence. Do I even belong in this field of work anymore? Yet I am still here on this earth.

I exist now just to find the settings that might make this phone work to some sort of normalcy. I am checking every setting and yet I find nothing but Bixby. Why can't I turn this off? Why can't I just use Android for maps, for texting, for anything? I am lost in an eternal abyss searching for something that I understand. I can't even type, "to" in a message because Bixby keeps thinking by swiping that I want TY... Then I realize someone in Samsung thought we should never say to, we should always say TY for some random reason... I don't even know what "TY" means. Am I this old, yes this is how it feels to use Samsung phone. Don't get me wrong the phone actually functions fine but it's so alien by default.

Once you get the settings off Bixby it's great. I finally figured out you have to download everything google then it actually works. The phone itself is actually good. The problem is you can't get rid of Bixby only set it to off by default. The programs will still take up space on your phone no matter what. Oh and don't even get me started on the wrap around screen that does nothing but interfere with fingers on the side... If you get a bulky enough case it sort of helps but did you even test this Samsung???
